| [LIT-046](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-046.md) v3 | The Computational Foundations of Collective Intelligence | Pilgrim et al. (2025), [ARXIV-2509.07999](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.07999). | [LIT-097](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-097.md) v3 | The Extended Mind | Clark & Chalmers (1998), DOI-10.1093/analys/58.1.7. The paper argues from a functionalist parity claim that a process or standing state which would count as cognitive if it happened in the head counts as cognitive when an external resource carries it, provided the resource is actively coupled to the organism here and now. | [LIT-105](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-105.md) v3 | On the Evolution, Science, and Metaphysics of Consciousness | Veit (2025), DOI-10.1177/10597123251413204. Veit's reply to five commentaries on *A Philosophy for the Science of Animal Consciousness* (2023). Its main new content is the metaphysics the book left to one paragraph. He says hedonic "feel" is *identical* with a valence system: "a common currency of sharing evaluative information across multiple control systems". The currency metaphor, he says, is "not Cartesian but cybernetic" (p. 10). He keeps the word "qualia", arguing that Cartesians have no "definitional rights" (p. 9), and he insists the pathological complexity thesis (PCT) is compatible with any metaphysics, dualism and panpsychism included (p. 9). Against his other critics, he defends a bottom-up evolutionary method that uses human data (de Weerd); a naturalism that is neither autopoietic nor biopsychist (Sachs); evaluation-first over prediction-first, consciousness as an adaptation, and graded, partial unity (Suzuki); and the link to welfare science (Chincarini). | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-187](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-187.md)); worth reading as the only extended statement of the metaphysics behind the pathological complexity thesis, and as the direct answer to Frankish ([LIT-103](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-103.md)). The reply to Frankish is the substantive part. The replies to de Weerd and Suzuki mostly restate the book's positions against objections quoted only in part, so read them alongside the commentaries. |

| [LIT-140](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-140.md) v2 | Large Language Models Are Stochastic Measuring Devices | Mallory (2025), DOI-10.1093/9780191998317.003.0003. The chapter argues by analogy that deep neural networks are "stochastic measuring devices". Training alters the parameters in response to data, so that the resulting configuration carries information about the data ("training is measurement"). The trained weights are a model, and generation is simulation. DNNs are stochastic because random initialisation and non-convex loss mean runs need not converge to the same weights, failing Baird's "regularity" condition. The problems of interpreting model states and generated text are therefore the familiar problems of instruments, models and simulations. The problem of interpretable AI is an instance of the coordination problem in the philosophy of measurement. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-090](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-090.md)); worth reading as the most developed instrument-centred alternative to agentive framings of LLMs, and for its tidy division into model-interpretation, text-interpretation and linking problems; it offers an analogy, not a refutation (its own words, § Interpretation and Communication), and should be read in the published OUP version where possible. |
| [LIT-147](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-147.md) v3 | Mental causation via neuroprosthetics? A critical analysis | Pernu (2018), DOI-10.1007/s11229-018-1713-z. The interventionist/difference-making case for nonreductive mental causation from BCIs (List & Menzies 2009; Menzies 2015; Woodward 2008a,b, 2017) misplaces multiple realisation. What the ensemble recordings show is that one cortical-level variable N (the ensemble's average firing) is realised by many single-neuron patterns N1, N2. Each intention M corresponds to one value of N. So the counterfactual contrast "∼M □→ ∼B true, ∼N □→ ∼B false" fails, and neuroprosthetics supports mental causation only by identifying M with N, not nonreductive physicalism. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-091](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-091.md)); Worth reading as a short, precise diagnosis of a specific equivocation in the interventionist BCI argument (multiple realisation at the wrong level). | [LIT-207](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-207.md) v2 | Talkative AI and the fiction of artificial minds | Roberts (2026), DOI-10.1007/s11098-026-02560-8. If a substantial class of mental states (interoceptive, affective, perceptual, and bodily-agentive states such as effort, trying and ownership) depends on an animate body, then today's disembodied chatbots lack them, and their many self-ascriptions of such states are "systematically untrue". He argues that this fictionalist stance escapes the epistemic norms that bind realist belief. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-157](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-157.md)); worth reading as a short, clear statement of chatbot fictionalism. | [LIT-212](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-212.md) v2 | Do Large Language Models Hallucinate Electric Fata Morganas? | Šekrst (2025), [ARXIV-2608.18816](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.18816). A conceptual essay whose one substantive thesis is this. Following Dziri et al., hallucination includes any output "not rooted in the model's source data", including expressed emotions and opinions (§6). An LLM's apparent inner life is therefore always a candidate hallucination, so any real AI consciousness "might always remain epistemically inaccessible" (§8). The empirical support is two unquantified anecdotes: a Titanic question put to gpt-3.5-turbo and GPT-4 at unstated temperatures, and an extractive-QA BERT mislabelled "WikiBERT". Its one idea, that self-reports of inner states are exactly what a system trained on human text would produce whether or not it has them, is a single paragraph's point. | [LIT-220](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-220.md) v2 | Real Patterns | Dennett (1991), DOI-10.2307/2027085. A pattern is real in some data "if there is a description of the data that is more efficient than the bit map, whether or not anyone can concoct it" (p. 34). This is Chaitin's incompressibility definition of randomness turned around (p. 32). Dennett uses the criterion, with the Game of Life's gliders and eaters as the stepping stone (pp. 37–42), to defend "mild realism" about beliefs. Folk psychology tracks a real, noisy pattern of enormous predictive leverage. Two rival interpretations can be "different, but equally real, patterns" with no deeper fact to settle between them (p. 49). | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-190](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-190.md)); Worth reading as the source of the real-patterns criterion that rainforest realism generalises into a theory of existence, and as the paper whose exact definition the later literature modifies. Its sharpest result is that the quantum question model's QQ equality implies noncontextuality, so the best-supported quantum-cognition model of order effects predicts its absence. First, prompted as test subjects on Aerts & Sozzo's "The Animal Acts" concept-combination test, ChatGPT and Gemini give CHSH values above 2: 4 in a guided conversation, and 2.25 and 3.09 (ChatGPT) and 2.12 and 4 (Gemini) over 81 prompted repetitions, against 2.42 for the 81 humans in 2011. The authors take these as showing that LLM "code is structurally quantum" (§5). The CHSH analysis never checks the strongly context-dependent marginals in its own tables. One reported expectation value disagrees with its table. The Bose–Einstein fit is numerically a Zipf–Mandelbrot law. | Rejected — read in full 2026-09-27 ([NOTE-243](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-243.md)); not worth a reader's time for its claims, because the data cannot carry them. | [LIT-312](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-312.md) v2 | A theory of concepts and their combinations II: A Hilbert space representation | Aerts & Gabora (2005), DOI-10.1108/03684920510575807. Aerts & Gabora embed the "pet" data in ℂ¹⁴⁰⁰. Each of 1,400 "basic contexts" is one vector of an orthonormal basis, the ground state is the uniform superposition, and each context is the projector onto the span of its basic contexts. The Born rule then returns the measured frequencies as counting ratios, for example cat under "chewing a bone" = 75/303 = 0.25. "Pet fish" is modelled as the entangled state Σ_{u∈E} \|u⟩⊗\|u⟩/√100 in ℂ¹⁴⁰⁰⊗ℂ⁴⁰⁸, so that collapsing "pet" to goldfish collapses "fish" to goldfish too. Every projector in the model is diagonal in one basis, so the fitted model is a classical probability space in quantum notation, which the authors half-concede (a "quantization … of this set theoretical model", §3.3). Two of the chosen counts are infeasible: parrot and guppy. | Active — read in full 2026-09-29 ([NOTE-299](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-299.md)); worth reading as the concrete source of the quantum-cognition treatment of concepts (projectors for contexts, collapse for context change, tensor product and entanglement for combination), and as an early proposal of tensor-product sentence meaning before DisCoCat. They then *postulate* that contexts and properties each form a complete orthocomplemented lattice, and call the structure quantum-like because a state can be an eigenstate of e ∨ f without being one of e or of f (eq. 19). No theorem is proved, the lattice is not shown to be non-distributive or orthomodular, and the paper contains no Hilbert-space model and no treatment of combination; both are deferred to Part II. | Active — read in full 2026-09-29 ([NOTE-294](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-294.md)); worth reading as the founding statement of the state-context-property approach to concepts that the prior-art map cites, and for its pet data. | [LIT-367](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-367.md) v2 | Calculation of signal detection theory measures | Stanislaw & Todorov (1999), DOI-10.3758/BF03207704. A practical tutorial that gives closed-form SDT measures computed from the hit rate H and false-alarm rate F. They are d′ = Φ⁻¹(H) − Φ⁻¹(F); β = exp{[Φ⁻¹(F)² − Φ⁻¹(H)²]/2}; c = −[Φ⁻¹(H) + Φ⁻¹(F)]/2; the nonparametric A′ and Grier's B″ (single-formula versions, eqs. 3 and 9); A_z = Φ(intercept/√(1+slope²)) from the z-ROC, whose slope is σ_noise/σ_signal; and A_d′ = Φ(d′/√2), which equals 2AFC proportion correct under the d′ assumptions. It also gives one-line commands for seven software packages. Its worked rating example (50 signal and 25 noise trials, noise SD larger than signal SD) shows d′ ranging from 0.84 to 1.86 across criteria. The authors conclude that d′ should not be used without rating-task evidence of equal variance. | Active — read in full 2026-09-30 ([NOTE-314](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-314.md)); worth reading as the standard short, citable reference for how the SDT measures are computed and what each assumes. It is a tutorial with no new theory. Several of its software pointers (1999 FTP sites, Quattro Pro, SYSTAT commands) are dated, but the formulae are not. |
| [LIT-368](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-368.md) v2 | A decision-making theory of visual detection | Tanner & Swets (1954), DOI-10.1037/h0058700. Tanner and Swets model visual detection as testing a statistical hypothesis. The observer compares one sample of neural activity with a cutoff, and signal+noise and noise are Gaussian with equal variance, separated by d′ (the mean difference in noise-SD units, defined as the square root of Peterson and Birdsall's d). The cutoff moves along a curve of P_SN(A) against P_N(A) (the curve now called the ROC; for d′ = 1 it passes through (.16, .50), (.50, .84) and (.84, .98)). The optimal operating point is where the slope equals β = [(1−P(SN))/P(SN)]·[(V_N·CA+K_N·A)/(V_SN·A+K_SN·CA)]. The 4AFC prediction is P(C)=∫F(x)³g(x)dx. With three paid observers, d′ estimated from yes-no data predicted 4AFC accuracy. The "false alarms are guesses" (high-threshold) hypothesis is rejected: false-alarm rate correlated with chance-corrected thresholds (ρ = .30, .71, .67; combined p ≪ .001), and all 12 fitted yes-no scatter lines miss the point (1, 1). | Active — read in full 2026-09-30 ([NOTE-316](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-316.md)); worth reading as the founding psychophysics paper of signal detection theory: it is short, it is the first place d′ is named, and it is the first to put the observer on the ROC and to set the likelihood-ratio criterion β from priors and payoffs. For the ideal-observer mathematics it defers entirely to Peterson and Birdsall (1953), and its experiment is small (three observers) with some statistics asserted rather than shown. |
| [LIT-373](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-373.md) v4 | The two dragons of cognition: recursive condensation for predictive processing | Li (2026), DOI-10.3389/fncom.2026.1778902. A "Hypothesis and Theory" essay proposing that the neocortex is a "biological Savitch machine". Alternating expansion ("odd parity") and contraction ("even parity") phases manufacture the disjoint closed sets of Urysohn's Lemma, and storing ("memoizing") the condensed tokens converts exponential search into polynomial "navigation". Its one non-standard formal result, Theorem 2, R(N) ∝ b^{αN} (§5.2.2, p. 11), is stated without proof. There is no data, simulation or model. The two mathematical pillars are misdescribed: Savitch's theorem saves space at the cost of time and does not memoize, and Urysohn's Lemma gives a continuous separator, not a linear one, and is not an "if and only if". | Rejected — re-read jointly with [LIT-374](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-374.md) and arXiv 2602.07974 on 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-321](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-321.md)); Read jointly with [LIT-374](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-374.md) and the companion StrLT preprint (arXiv 2602.07974), the essay is the cognitive motivation of a coherent programme: structure is discovered by costly search, condensed into frozen tokens, and reused cheaply. It is not just a misuse of two theorems. Read charitably, its mathematical slips are repairable and are not the reason to set it aside: the Urysohn "iff" and linear readout, Savitch as memoisation, the Definition 2 clash. The reason is what is left after repair: an amortised-inference and complementary-learning-systems picture already in the literature it cites; a neural mapping whose predictions do not discriminate it from standard consolidation accounts; one original quantitative claim, Theorem 2, that is not argued. A reader who wants the programme should read [LIT-374](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-374.md) and the companion, where it is made precise. |
| [LIT-374](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-374.md) v3 | Structural Decoupling: A Scaffold-Flow Theory of Generalization and Alignment | Li (2026), arXiv:2506.20699. 'Proposes "width", the least number of cells in an open cover on each of which some predictor is γ-contractive with conditional risk ≤ δ, as a structural complexity separate from VC dimension. From an additive Rademacher bound, √(2d_str log(e(K−1)n/d_str)/n) + LK·R_n(G) (Thm 4.5), it argues that context routing (the "scaffold") should be trained by different signals from within-context prediction (the "flow"), and that alignment failures are scaffold failures. The routine results are proved: coupon-collector Ω(w log w), Lipschitz composition, penalised model selection, multiclass Sauer–Shelah. The new ones are not. The phase transition at width is assumed in its proof. The bouquet witness of width/VC separation contradicts its own construction. The "fundamental theorem" is false as stated, because infinite pseudo-dimension does not prevent learnability. No theorem links the CS-Laplacian estimator to width. There are no experiments.' | Proposed — re-read jointly with [LIT-373](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-373.md) and arXiv 2602.07974 on 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-322](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-322.md)); promising and unproven. Read jointly with the companion arXiv 2602.07974, which carries the fuller statements and several definitions this paper leaves implicit. The formal core holds in repaired form: width as a structural complexity incomparable with the per-cell VC dimension; an error floor below width; the Ω(w log w) discovery cost; an additive Rademacher bound for routed predictors. The flagged slips are repairable and not load-bearing: the bouquet cover, the non-degeneracy assumption in the appendix, Massart, and pseudo-dimension against fat-shattering in Thm 4.6. What remains unproven are the claims that would make it matter: that the CS estimator converges to width itself and not to a predictor-relative count; that a monolithic model cannot match K ≥ w routing; above all, that router/scaffold training should be decoupled from task loss. This is presented as derived from the additive bound, but the bound holds for joint training too. The alignment section is asserted. What would settle it: on synthetic benchmarks of known width, (i) a K-sweep showing the floor at K < w for routed learners and its absence or presence for capacity-matched monolithic models; (ii) CS width recovery from a cold start; (iii) decoupled against joint router training, compared on forgetting and boundary error. |
| [LIT-377](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-377.md) | On Context-Content Uncertainty Principle | Li (2025), arXiv:2506.20699 v1. It posits that structured content (priors, schemas) has far lower entropy than context (sensory input), and concludes that inference should run from content to context, minimizing H(context \| content). On that it builds four layers of principles. The first is structure before specificity and its equivalents. The second covers precision-weighted attention, slower learning for content than for context, and memory as low-entropy attractors. The third is staged structure-first learning, and the fourth hierarchical composition. It then reads predictive coding, the free energy principle, active inference and attractor dynamics as instances. Everything is asserted or argued informally. There are no experiments, and several proofs are wrong or missing. | Rejected — by [LIT-374](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-374.md); read in full 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-325](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-325.md)); not worth a reader's time as a source of results. Its foundation is the entropy chain rule plus an assumption, H(content) ≪ H(context), and from these it reads off a direction of inference. Of its eight theorems, one is proved only in sketch, one equivalence proposition is marked "proof skipped" and argued only in words (App. H), and the proofs of Theorems 6–8 swap the roles of content and context relative to the statements. The proof of Theorem 1 states the inequality backwards. Theorem 3 rests on D_KL(q‖p) ≥ H(q) − H(p), which is false in general. The abstract's "computational simulations" are not in the paper. The author's own v2 (June 2026) replaced the whole framework under a new title. |
| [LIT-383](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-383.md) | Deciding Advantageously Before Knowing the Advantageous Strategy | Bechara, H. Damasio, Tranel & A. R. Damasio (1997), DOI-10.1126/science.275.5304.1293. In the four-deck gambling task, 10 controls and 6 ventromedial prefrontal patients were tracked on choices, anticipatory skin-conductance responses and verbal reports. All controls and no patients developed anticipatory responses; controls came to prefer the good decks, significantly from the point they reported a hunch; three patients who could state the correct strategy kept choosing the bad decks. The authors conclude that nonconscious biases guide behaviour before conscious knowledge does. The statistics support the group difference more firmly than the "before knowing" timing. | Active — read in full 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-331](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-331.md)); worth reading as the experiment the somatic marker hypothesis is usually cited for, and worth reading with its notes, which are weaker than its abstract. With 10 controls and 6 ventromedial patients, the robust results are that every control and no patient developed anticipatory skin-conductance responses, and that three patients who could state the right strategy still chose badly. The headline that controls chose well and responded to risky decks "before they knew" is only partly carried by the statistics: in the pre-hunch period the controls' preference for the good decks was not significant (note 9), and the reported SCR effect there is a group-by-period interaction, not a bad-versus-good-deck difference (note 8). Controls chose the good decks significantly only once they reported a hunch. Whether the account is true is not this note's question. |
| [LIT-384](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-384.md) | The somatic marker hypothesis and the possible functions of the prefrontal cortex | Damasio (1996), DOI-10.1098/rstb.1996.0125. States the somatic marker hypothesis: ventromedial prefrontal cortex holds learned links between classes of situation and the body states (emotions) that went with them; when a situation recurs, those states are re-enacted, through the body or through an "as if" loop in somatosensory cortex, and mark imagined option-outcome pairs as good or bad, overtly as a feeling or covertly as a bias, so that reasoning works over a pruned space. Evidence summarised: ventromedial patients with intact intellect decide badly in life, lack skin-conductance responses to emotive pictures, and in the gambling task keep choosing the losing decks and show no anticipatory responses. | Active — read in full 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-332](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-332.md)); worth reading as the shortest statement of the somatic marker hypothesis by its author, with the evidence it then rested on. It is a hypothesis paper: the mechanism (ventromedial prefrontal linkages that re-enact body states, by a "body loop" or an "as if body loop", which then mark options good or bad) is stated, not shown, and the evidence it reports is lesion and skin-conductance work summarised from other papers, without numbers. Its strongest piece, that ventromedial patients lack anticipatory skin-conductance responses in the gambling task while responding normally to the losses themselves, is reported here in one paragraph; the 1997 Science report filed alongside it is the place to see that result. Whether the account is true is not this note's question. |
| [LIT-385](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-385.md) | Time-locked multiregional retroactivation: A systems-level proposal for the neural substrates of recall and recognition | Damasio (1989), Cognition 33:25–62. The convergence-zone proposal: memory is not held in one store but as feature fragments in early sensory and motor cortices, with amodal records of their co-occurrence held in local and non-local convergence zones downstream; recall is the time-locked reactivation of the fragments, directed from convergence zones through feedback projections. Unread: registered from the abstract. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-01 at the owner's request for Antonio Damasio's work; no full text could be reached (the Elsevier article is closed, and no repository, author or course copy was found), so it is registered from its PubMed abstract only, unread, and no NOTE is filed |
| [LIT-392](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-392.md) | Absent Qualia, Fading Qualia, Dancing Qualia | Chalmers (1995), in T. Metzinger (ed.), Conscious Experience (Imprint Academic, co-published in Paderborn). Principle: any system with the same fine-grained functional organisation as a conscious system has qualitatively identical experiences. Replace neurons gradually with silicon chips that keep the organisation. If the end point lacked experience, a midpoint would be a rational being wrong about all its experience ("fading qualia"). If it differed in experience, a switch between two circuits would flip experience with no possible noticing ("dancing qualia"). Both are judged implausible, so absent and inverted qualia are nomologically impossible. The argument extends explicitly to a population of homunculi. The result is "nonreductive functionalism": organisation fixes experience with natural, not metaphysical, necessity. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-347](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-347.md)); worth reading as the full statement of the principle of organizational invariance and the fading- and dancing-qualia arguments for it. Cite it carefully: the principle is conditional on fine-grained functional isomorphism to a system already conscious. It covers silicon replacement and, by the paper's own §3 extension, a population of homunculi that implements a human's neural organisation. It does not cover a system whose organisation is merely similar in kind to a conscious one, so it does not license Schwitzgebel's step to the United States ([LIT-159](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-159.md)). The conclusion is nomological, not metaphysical ("nonreductive functionalism"), and it is a plausibility argument by the author's own account. |

By Stich's 1980 summary, which Dennett accepted: the worry that internal representations need a homunculus to read them ("Hume's Problem") is unfounded, because homunculi are harmless if they are stupider than the whole. A "team or committee of relatively ignorant, narrow-minded, blind homunculi" can produce intelligent behaviour, each explained by stupider ones, until they can be "replaced by a machine"; AI organises "armies of such idiots". | Deferred — registered 2026-10-02 from catalogue records and a contemporary summary, not read: no lawful full text could be reached. Brainstorms (1978) is lending-only at the Internet Archive, the MIT Press and Project MUSE chapters are paywalled (MUSE: "Open Access: No"), the Tufts Digital Library holds Dennett's papers but not this essay, and PhilPapers was blocked. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-394](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-394.md) | Computing Machinery and Intelligence | Turing (1950), Mind 59(236):433–460. "Can machines think?" is replaced by whether a digital computer can play the imitation game so that an interrogator, questioning by teleprinter, identifies it no more reliably than he tells a man from a woman. Universality reduces the question to one computer suitably programmed. Turing predicts that by about 2000 a machine with 10^9 bits of storage will leave an average interrogator no more than a 70 per cent chance of a right identification after five minutes. He answers nine objections, the argument from consciousness by its collapse into solipsism, and proposes reaching the goal by educating a child-machine. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-355](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-355.md)); worth reading as the source of the imitation game and as the first catalogue of objections to machine thought, nine of them, each still argued. Read it for what it actually proposes: not a definition of thinking but the replacement of an ill-posed question by a test, a prediction about 2000 (70 per cent right identification after five minutes, at 10^9 bits), and a programme for reaching it by educating a child-machine. Its reply to the argument from consciousness is an other-minds argument, not a theory of consciousness, and Turing says outright that he does not think there is "no mystery about consciousness". |
| [LIT-396](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-396.md) | Psychological Predicates | Putnam (1967), in Capitan & Merrill (eds.), Art, Mind, and Religion (Proceedings of the 1965 Oberlin Colloquium in Philosophy), University of Pittsburgh Press, pp. 37–48; reprinted as "The Nature of Mental States". It proposes, as an empirical hypothesis, that pain is a functional state of a whole organism, a state of a probabilistic automaton fixed by its machine table, rather than a brain state. Condition (3) of the hypothesis is the anti-nesting stipulation: no pain-feeler "possesses a decomposition into parts which separately possess Descriptions" of the pain-capable kind, introduced only "to rule out such 'organisms' (if they can count as such) as swarms of bees as single pain-feelers". | Deferred — not read in full: the original (Art, Mind, and Religion, pp. 37–48) is closed on JSTOR. The University of Pittsburgh's page images sit behind a bot challenge I could not pass, and the Internet Archive copy of the 1975 reprint is print-disabled only. What was read is MIT's 24.09x course excerpt of the 1975 reprint ("The Nature of Mental States"), recorded as a Skimmed reading in [NOTE-335](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-335.md). That excerpt carries the four-clause hypothesis verbatim, including the anti-nesting condition (3) and its one-sentence motive. |
| [LIT-398](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-398.md) | True Believers: The Intentional Strategy and Why It Works | Dennett (1981; revised 1987, read in Mind Design II, 1997). Belief is "a perfectly objective phenomenon" that can be discerned only by one who adopts the intentional strategy. To be a true believer is to be a system "whose behavior is reliably and voluminously predictable" by it. The choice of stance is free, but its success is objective: Laplacean Martians who skipped it would miss real patterns. Thermostat and person differ only by degree. Why the strategy works is answered easily by evolution, and not yet at all by mechanism. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-353](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-353.md)), in the revised text reprinted in Mind Design II (1997), not the 1981 printing; worth reading as Dennett's statement that belief is objective although only visible through a strategy: anything whose behaviour is "reliably and voluminously predictable" by the intentional strategy is a believer "in the fullest sense of the word". It turns the 1971 paper's observer-relativity ([LIT-440](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-440.md)) into "the facts about the success or failure of the stance … are perfectly objective", introduces the Martian thought experiment and the intentional "real patterns" later worked out in [LIT-220](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-220.md), and runs the thermostat-to-person continuum ("no magic moment"). Its criterion admits any system on which the strategy pays, groups included, but the essay never applies it to a group. |
| [LIT-399](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-399.md) | Plain Talk About Neurodevelopmental Epistemology | Minsky (1977), MIT AI Memo 430, also IJCAI-77 pp. 1083–1092. Takes the mind as an organised society of simple "agents", a theory credited to joint work with Papert, and asks how such agents could communicate without language. The proposal: no messages at all, since each argument lives at a fixed location on shared channels ("c-lines") that the agents themselves constitute as short-term memory. A specificity gradient confines low-level agents to local sub-societies, and a case-shift moves an object of attention into a better-described slot. The paper conjectures that these internal cases precede, and shape, the cases of natural language. Openly speculative. | Active — read in full 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-344](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-344.md)); worth reading as the earliest of Minsky's own papers in this record to state the society-of-agents view, then called "The Society of Minds" (Note 1), and as its first worked mechanism: agents communicate by fixed-location channels ("c-lines") instead of messages. It is openly speculative ("a model of scientific irresponsibility", p. 1085), with no data and no program. Read it for the communication scheme, the "specificity gradient", the case-shift mechanism and the conjecture that cognitive cases precede and shape linguistic ones; do not read it as evidence for any of them. That it is the first published statement of the idea is the usual attribution, and this reading could not confirm it (see [NOTE-344](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-344.md)). |
| [LIT-400](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-400.md) | Minds, brains, and programs | Searle (1980), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 3(3):417–424. A man who knows no Chinese, locked in a room with rules in English for manipulating Chinese symbols, can answer Chinese questions as well as a native speaker yet understands nothing; so instantiating a program is never by itself sufficient for intentionality ("strong AI" is false). Six replies are answered, the systems reply by letting the man internalise the whole room. Only something with causal powers equivalent to a brain's could think; programs have syntax but no semantics. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-349](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-349.md)); worth reading as the source of the Chinese room and of the six replies (systems, robot, brain simulator, combination, other minds, many mansions) the debate still uses, in Searle's own words. Read it for its scope: the target is "strong AI", the claim that instantiating the right program is by itself sufficient for understanding, and Searle grants that machines, including artifacts with the brain's causal powers, could think. The argument is about understanding and intentionality; consciousness is mentioned, not argued. Its answer to the systems reply (internalise the room) is the part that bears on minds of parts, and it is asserted rather than shown: Searle says the subsystem is "simply a part of" the man, which is what the reply denies. |
| [LIT-402](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-402.md) | K-Lines: A Theory of Memory | Minsky (1979/1980), MIT AI Memo 516; Cognitive Science 4(2):117–133. "The function of a memory is to re-create a state of mind." On a memorable event a K-node is made, and its K-line attaches to the agents then active. Reactivated, it re-imposes that partial mental state, but by the level-band principle only on an intermediate band of levels, so the present is seen as an instance of the past without hallucinating the old answer. K-lines attach mainly to earlier K-nodes, forming a K-pyramid against the perceptual P-pyramid, and cross-exclusion lets conflicting details cancel into abstraction. Read from the memo; a programme statement, with no simulation. | Active — read in full 2026-10-01 from the MIT AI Memo 516 text ([NOTE-352](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-352.md)), not the Cognitive Science version, which was not reachable; worth reading as the society-of-mind programme's theory of memory and the first place Minsky's own text uses the phrase "Society of Mind". The idea to take away is that a memory re-creates a partial mental state rather than retrieving a stored description, and its level-band principle: re-enact only an intermediate band of the original state, so the present problem is seen as an instance of the remembered one. The second half is, by its author's account, not constructive ("from this point, the reader can assume that difficulties in understanding are my fault"), and nothing is simulated or measured. |
| [LIT-403](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-403.md) | Intrinsic content, active memory and the extended mind | Clark (2005), DOI-10.1093/analys/65.1.1. Against Adams & Aizawa: the intrinsic-content objection to [LIT-097](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-097.md) fails, because the notion is unclear, silicon parts could carry it, and a conventional encoding linked at run-time to intrinsically contentful states can be a belief's vehicle, inside or outside the head. Against the active-memory objection, the notebook's passivity is a difference below the functional level that matters. The extended mind is a thesis about vehicles. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-363](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-363.md)); worth reading as Clark's first reply to the critics of [LIT-097](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-097.md), and short. It answers Adams and Aizawa's intrinsic-content objection three ways (the notion is unclear, silicon could carry it, and it would not matter), turning their own concession that not every cognitive state needs non-derived content against them; and it answers the "active memory" objection by conceding the notebook is unlike biological memory and arguing that the differences sit below the level a functionalist should attend to. Its replies are parity arguments with imagined cases; it adds no new evidence. It does not engage Rupert ([LIT-422](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-422.md)). |
| [LIT-404](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-404.md) | Does a rock implement every finite-state automaton? | Chalmers (1996), Synthese 108(3):309–333. Putnam's proof that every open system implements every finite-state automaton fails, because implementation needs reliable, counterfactual-supporting transitions for every formal state. Repaired, it survives only for weak formalisms: a clock and a dial implement every inputless FSA, and an input memory and a dial upgrade any system with the right input–output dependencies to every FSA with them. Combinatorial-state automata, whose states are vectors of independently varying components in distinct physical regions, put a strong constraint on implementation. That keeps computation available as a foundation for the theory of mind. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-342](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-342.md)), from the author's HTML copy, not the Synthese typeset text; worth reading as the standard reply to Putnam's and Searle's triviality arguments and as the source of the combinatorial-state automaton (CSA). Its result is real but partial: implementation needs counterfactual-supporting transitions over all formal states, inputless FSAs are trivially implemented by any clock plus dial, FSAs with input are implemented by any system with the right input–output dependencies plus an input memory and a dial, and CSAs escape only because a blind implementation must grow by a factor of n per step. Chalmers leaves two open problems (logically possible false implementations, and an overstrict one-region-per-component condition). For this record it decides which formalism a China-brain argument has to be stated in, and it lets one physical system host two minds. |
| [LIT-406](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-406.md) | Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness | Chalmers (1995), Journal of Consciousness Studies 2(3):200–219. The "easy" problems of consciousness (discrimination, integration, report, access, attention, control, wakefulness) are problems of explaining functions, and a mechanism that performs a function explains it. The hard problem is that after every such function is explained, "why is the performance of these functions accompanied by experience?" stays open, so reductive methods cannot answer it. Experience should be taken as fundamental, linked to the physical by psychophysical laws. Two nonbasic candidates are offered, structural coherence (the structure of experience mirrors the structure of awareness) and organizational invariance (fine-grained functional isomorphs have the same experiences), with a speculative double-aspect theory of information as the basic law. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-336](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-336.md)); worth reading as the source of the easy/hard distinction, and short. Cite it for three separable things: the hard problem as the claim that explaining every function near experience leaves "why is this accompanied by experience?" open (§§2–3); the outline of a nonreductive theory built from two nonbasic principles, structural coherence and organizational invariance (§7); and the double-aspect theory of information, which the author calls "more of an idea than a theory" (§8). The organizational-invariance argument here is a one-page sketch; the full version is [LIT-392](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-392.md). |
| [LIT-407](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-407.md) | Troubles with Functionalism | Block (1978), Minnesota Studies in the Philosophy of Science 9:261–325. Functionalism ties mental states to the world only through inputs and outputs, so it is "liberal": a body run by a billion people with radios, each implementing one line of your machine table (the nation-of-China system), would be functionally equivalent to you, yet there is prima facie doubt that it has qualia. Putnam's stipulation that no pain-feeler has parts with pain-feeler organisation is an ad hoc patch that fails on its own terms. Psychofunctionalism escapes the doubt for beliefs but perhaps not for qualia, and no specification of inputs and outputs avoids both liberalism and chauvinism. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-366](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-366.md)); worth reading as the source of the homunculi-headed robot and the nation-of-China system, and of the first published objection to Putnam's anti-nesting stipulation. Cite it for two things that are easy to run together: the Absent Qualia Argument (a Functional simulation built from people is prima facie without qualia), and the case that Putnam's condition is ad hoc (§1.5). Block grounds the doubt about the China system in its being unlike us psychologically and neurally and designed to mimic us, not in its parts having minds (n. 19). He also grants that a Psychofunctional homunculi-head could have beliefs (§2.1). So it is not a source for "a whole made of minded parts cannot be conscious". |
| [LIT-408](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-408.md) | Jokes and the Logic of the Cognitive Unconscious | Minsky (1980), MIT AI Memo 603; in Vaina & Hintikka (eds.), Cognitive Constraints on Communication (Reidel, 1984), pp. 175–200. Commonsense logic cannot be made reliable, so each mind accumulates "censors" that learn the precursors of known-bad thought (paradox, circling, false analogy) and suppress it before it occurs. On that view, humour is censor-learning. Its common element is an "unexpected frame-substitution", and laughter both stops the absurd line of thought and holds it in focus. Logical nonsense is then as "naughty" as Freud's forbidden wishes, which removes the gap in Freud's theory. An essay with no data or program. | Active — read in full 2026-10-01 from the MIT AI Memo 603 text ([NOTE-361](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-361.md)), not the 1984 book chapter, which was not reachable; worth reading as the society-of-mind programme's account of humour and of "negative meta-knowledge". Its argument is that commonsense reasoning cannot be made reliable, so minds learn "censors" that suppress known-bad lines of thought, and that humour and laughter are how those censors are taught and engaged, which dissolves Freud's puzzle about nonsense jokes. It is an essay: no data, no program, and its evolutionary story is offered as "no plea for this particular scenario". |
| [LIT-410](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-410.md) | A Framework for Representing Knowledge | Minsky (1974), MIT AI Memo 306. A self-declared partial theory of thinking: on meeting a situation one retrieves a frame, a stereotyped structure whose terminals carry conditions and weakly bound default assignments, and adapts it by replacing details. Frames that share terminals form frame-systems whose transformations stand for moves, actions or changes of viewpoint, and failed matches are routed through a learned similarity network. The memo applies this to vision, imagery, language, memory and problem solving, and ends by arguing that consistency-seeking logical systems cannot represent commonsense knowledge, because they are monotonic. Nothing is implemented or tested. | Active — read in full 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-337](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-337.md)); worth reading as the source of the frame idea and of the critique of "logistic" representation that later motivated non-monotonic reasoning. It is a proposal, not a result: no program is described as built, nothing is measured, and the author says so ("Apology!", p. 2). The parts to take away are the frame with weakly bound default assignments (§1.11), frame-systems sharing terminals across viewpoints (§1), terminals read as questions (§2.8), the similarity network with cluster "capitols" as an account of family resemblance (§§3.4–3.5), and the appendix on monotonicity and consistency (§6). It contains no society-of-agents idea; that arrives in Plain Talk ([LIT-399](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-399.md)), which calls itself in part a sequel to this memo. |
| [LIT-411](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-411.md) | Could a Large Language Model be Conscious? | Chalmers (2023), arXiv:2303.07103; Boston Review, 9 August 2023; from a NeurIPS 2022 invited talk. Asks for a feature X that LLMs have (or lack) and that indicates consciousness (or its absence). Self-report, seeming-conscious, conversation and general intelligence give at most weak evidence for it. Biology, senses and embodiment, world and self models, recurrent processing, a global workspace and unified agency are the evidence against. All but biology are temporary. On mainstream assumptions: under 10% credence for current LLMs, 25% or more for conscious LLM+ systems within a decade. Twelve challenges are offered as roadmap or red flags. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-345](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-345.md)), from arXiv v3 (the Boston Review text), with v1's conclusions compared; worth reading as the clearest short statement of the case for and against consciousness in LLMs, and as the origin of the "theory-balanced" credence approach that Butlin et al. built on. Its method is a regimented request for a feature X, and its verdicts are credences offered "for illustrative purposes": under 10% for current LLMs, 25% or more for conscious LLM+ systems within a decade, on "mainstream assumptions". It does not break the deadlock [THEORY-023](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-023.md) describes. It is an instance of it: mimicry undercuts self-report, the main obstacles are theory-derived, and biology is set aside rather than answered. |
| [LIT-412](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-412.md) | Supersizing the Mind: Embodiment, Action, and Cognitive Extension | Clark (2008), DOI-10.1093/acprof:oso/9780195333213.001.0001. Clark's book-length defence of the extended mind: a tour of embodied, situated and extended cognition, a reply to its critics, and a case for treating "some coalitions of biological and non-biological resources as the extended cognitive circuitry of individual minds". Unread: filed from the publisher's description and contents. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's abstract, its chapter list and its two front- and back-matter pieces that this record holds separately; the book's full text is not lawfully readable online, so it was not read and no NOTE is filed |
| [LIT-413](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-413.md) | The Mind's I: Fantasies and Reflections on Self and Soul | Hofstadter & Dennett (eds.) (1981), Basic Books. An anthology of 27 selections, fiction and philosophy, on self, soul and consciousness, each followed by a "Reflections" by the editors. Among them are Turing's imitation-game paper ([LIT-394](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-394.md)), Searle's Chinese room ([LIT-400](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-400.md)), Nagel's bat ([LIT-096](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-096.md)), Dennett's "Where Am I?" and Hofstadter's "Prelude ... Ant Fugue" from GEB ([LIT-437](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-437.md)). Unread: registered from the catalogue record and a contents note; the Reflections, which are the editors' own contribution, were not seen. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-02 from the Library of Congress catalogue record, the publisher's page and a library contents note, not read: no lawful full text could be reached. The Internet Archive scans of the 1981 Basic Books, Harvester, Bantam and Penguin printings are all lending-only, HathiTrust has no record for the LCCN, and no publisher, editor or Tufts-archive copy is posted. The editors' Reflections are unread. Two of the selections were read in full from lawful copies of their first publications and filed on their own: Turing ([LIT-394](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-394.md)) and Searle ([LIT-400](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-400.md)). |
| [LIT-414](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-414.md) | High-level perception, representation, and analogy: A critique of artificial intelligence methodology | Chalmers, French & Hofstadter (1992), DOI-10.1080/09528139208953747. Traditional AI hands its programs representations built by people who already know the answer, so models like BACON (Kepler's third law) and the Structure-Mapping Engine (atom and solar system) skip the hard part, high-level perception: deciding what is relevant and how to organise it. Nor can the gap be filled later by a separate "representation module", because analogy shapes perception and the task decides which representation is right. Copycat, in a microdomain of letter strings, is offered as an architecture that builds representations and mappings together. | Active — read in full 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-359](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-359.md)), from the authors' preprint (CRCC Technical Report 49, March 1991) that Chalmers posts; the published text was not seen. Worth reading as the clearest short statement of the Fluid Analogies Research Group's case against hand-coded representations, and as the most accessible description of Copycat. It is an argument, not a result: its two arguments against a separate "representation module" are informal and good, its case studies (BACON, SME) are fair as far as they go, and the evidence it offers for Copycat is a description of the architecture and one worked problem, with nothing measured in the paper itself. |
| [LIT-415](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-415.md) | Extended Cognition and Extended Consciousness | Chalmers (2019), DOI-10.1093/oso/9780190662813.003.0002. The 1998 extended-mind thesis as stated is too weak, since opponents accept extension in wired-in "extended circuit" cases. The interesting thesis is that mental states can be partly constituted by external entities in virtue of the subject's sensorimotor interaction with them. Consciousness does not extend this way, on the proposal that it requires information directly available for global control, and perceptually mediated availability is indirect. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-356](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-356.md)); worth reading as Chalmers's own later statement of what the extended-mind thesis of [LIT-097](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-097.md) is and where it stops. It does two things. It replaces the 1998 paper's implicit thesis, which it concedes is too weak because even the critics accept it for wired-in "extended circuit" cases, with one that requires constitution "in virtue of the subject's sensorimotor interaction" (§1). And it argues that consciousness does not extend, because consciousness needs information directly available for global control and perception makes availability indirect (§3). Both are proposals, argued in a short chapter: the thesis is offered as "extensionally correct", and the directness account is offered as an explanation of why there are no plausible cases, not as a knockdown. |
| [LIT-416](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-416.md) | Is there an 'I' in AI? | Hofstadter (2026), DOI-10.1098/rsta.2024.0527. The lead essay of the Phil. Trans. A theme issue on world models whose editorial is [LIT-195](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-195.md). Unread: what is known of it here comes from the editorial as read in [NOTE-136](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-136.md), which quotes Hofstadter that a system passing a Turing test of consistent understanding should be credited with thinking, and that conscious AI may come "perhaps even by 2033". Whether the essay argues "nearly the opposite" of the editors' convergence verdict cannot be checked until the essay itself is read. | Deferred — seeded 2026-10-01 from Crossref, PubMed and the record's reading of the theme-issue editorial ([LIT-195](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-195.md), [NOTE-136](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-136.md)), not read: royalsocietypublishing.org returned 403 to the DOI, article and PDF URLs, the article is not in PubMed Central or Europe PMC full text, and no repository or author copy was found. No NOTE is filed. |
| [LIT-417](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-417.md) | Epilogue: Analogy as the Core of Cognition | Hofstadter (2001), DOI-10.7551/mitpress/1251.003.0020. The epilogue to Gentner, Holyoak & Kokinov's The Analogical Mind (MIT Press), pp. 499–538, whose title states the Fluid Analogies Research Group's thesis that analogy-making is not one cognitive tool among others but the core of cognition. Unread: no lawful full text was reached. | Deferred — seeded 2026-10-01 from Crossref and the MIT Press chapter record, not read: MIT Press Direct returned 403 to the chapter PDF and book page, OpenAlex lists the chapter as closed access, and no author or institutional copy was found. Third-party copies exist (a personal reference collection and an Internet Archive upload) but neither is the author's or the publisher's, so neither was used. No NOTE is filed. |
| [LIT-418](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-418.md) | Society of mind: A response to four reviews | Minsky (1991), Artificial Intelligence 48(3):371–396. Minsky's reply, closing a review symposium, to four reviews of The Society of Mind in the same issue: by Michael G. Dyer, Matthew Ginsberg, George N. Reeke and Stephen W. Smoliar. Unread: the article is closed access and no copy was reached. Singh (2003) quotes it on why Minsky kept the words "agent" and "agency", and draws on it for a mechanism by which agents with different representations could communicate. | Deferred — seeded 2026-10-01 from the Crossref and Elsevier metadata of the article and of the issue it closes, not read: the article is closed access (Unpaywall and OpenAlex find no open copy, Semantic Scholar marks it closed, ScienceDirect refused the request), and no author copy was found. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. The four reviews it answers are listed below from the issue's contents, and are not filed. |
| [LIT-419](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-419.md) | Form, Function, and Feel | Lycan (1981), The Journal of Philosophy 78(1):24–50, DOI-10.2307/2025395. Filed as a statement of homuncular functionalism, the view Lycan's Wikipedia entry says he advocates, and as the reply Schwitzgebel points to against Block's nation-of-China intuition. Unread: no lawful full text was reachable, so its arguments are not stated here. | Deferred — seeded 2026-10-02 from the bibliographic records (Crossref, the Philosophy Documentation Center), not read: no lawful full text could be reached. JSTOR and PDC are paywalled, Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar list no open copy, and no author copy was found. No NOTE is filed. What it argues is known here only from how Schwitzgebel and Block's acknowledgements place it, which is not a reading. |
| [LIT-420](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-420.md) v2 | Surfaces and Essences: Analogy as the Fuel and Fire of Thinking | Hofstadter & Sander (2013), Basic Books. The book defends "the simple but unorthodox premise" that "analogy is the core of all thinking": analogy operates at every moment, from the choice of a word to the insights of physics, and is not a rare tool for hard problems. Its ten contents entries run from the evocation of words and phrases, through abstraction, "inter-category sliding" and naïve analogies, to "Analogies that shook the world" and a closing debate on the core of cognition. Unread: registered from the publisher's description and the catalogue's contents note. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-01 from the publisher's description and the Library of Congress catalogue record with its contents note, not read: no lawful full text could be reached. The Internet Archive scan is lending-only, and the full texts circulating online are not the publisher's or the authors'. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-421](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-421.md) | Foreword | Chalmers (2008), DOI-10.1093/acprof:oso/9780195333213.002.0007. The co-author's retrospective on the extended mind: his iPhone is "part of my mind already". The one principled objection is that perception and action bound the mental. His reply is revisionist and contextualist: whether Otto's belief counts as extended flips with explanatory purpose. No Otto-style twin case works for consciousness, so he tentatively keeps an internal conscious core. The thesis needs only a weak, parity-style functionalism and is compatible with dualism. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-369](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-369.md)); worth reading as the shortest statement of where Chalmers stands on the thesis he co-authored, ten years on. Three things in eight pages: the iPhone as a present-day Otto's notebook; the perception-action boundary as the one principled objection, answered by explanatory revisionism and a "Necker cube" view on which whether Otto's belief is extended depends on explanatory purpose; and a tentative internal "conscious core", resting on the failure of any Otto-style twin case for consciousness. It is a foreword: every position is stated briefly and several are offered as "perhaps". |
| [LIT-422](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-422.md) | Challenges to the Hypothesis of Extended Cognition | Rupert (2004), DOI-10.5840/jphil2004101826. The embedded hypothesis (HEMC: cognition leans heavily on external props, but is the organism's) competes with the extended one (HEC), and conservatism favours HEMC unless HEC buys explanatory power. It does not. [LIT-097](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-097.md)'s criteria either make phone directories into beliefs or privilege the organism, and memory research (interference, the generation effect, conversation) shows internal and external storage are different kinds. A generic kind covering both does no work. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-343](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-343.md)), in the author's pre-publication version; worth reading as the case that a conservative "embedded" hypothesis explains everything the extended hypothesis does, and as the empirical version of the critique. Its two arguments: a dilemma on [LIT-097](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-097.md)'s past-endorsement criterion (keep it and the organism is privileged after all; drop it and directory assistance gives Otto beliefs about every listed phone number), and memory research (interference, the generation effect, conversation) showing internal and external storage behave as different kinds, so that a kind covering both does no explanatory work. Its strength is that it argues from cognitive science rather than intuition; its limit is that the empirical differences are about fine-grained profiles, which a defender can accept and still claim a coarse kind. |
| [LIT-423](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-423.md) | I Am a Strange Loop | Hofstadter (2007), Basic Books. Per its publisher, an "I" is "a strange loop where the brain's symbolic and physical levels feed back into each other and flip causality upside down", and the book asks whether that "I" is real or "merely a convenient fiction", and how selves "can exist in the minds of others". Its 26 contents entries run from souls and the causal potency of patterns, through Gödel's "quintessential strange loop" and downward causality, to "How we live in each other", "Consciousness = thinking" and zombies and dualism. The Internet Archive scans are lending-only, and no publisher or author copy is posted. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-424](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-424.md) | From Bacteria to Bach and Back: The Evolution of Minds | Dennett (2017), W. W. Norton. Per its publisher, the book shows "step by step, how a comprehending mind could in fact have arisen from a mindless process of natural selection", with the decisive shift the sharing of memes, which produced "thinking tools" powerful enough that minds "create and comprehend". Its contents run from the origin of reasons and "two strange inversions of reasoning", through information, "brains made of brains", words, memes and the origins of language, to consciousness as "an evolved user-illusion" and "the age of post-intelligent design". | [LIT-425](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-425.md) | The Meta-Problem of Consciousness | Chalmers (2018), Journal of Consciousness Studies 25(9–10):6–61. The meta-problem is to explain, in terms that do not mention consciousness, why we judge that consciousness poses a hard problem. It is an "easy" problem with an empirical programme. Of thirteen candidate mechanisms, the most promising is an introspective model that attributes primitive relations of awareness to primitive qualities, with a sense of acquaintance. A realist theory should explain how its basis of consciousness produces these judgments, which IIT and biological theories struggle to do. Debunking arguments for illusionism can be blocked, but a residual sense of coincidence remains. Only strong illusionism dissolves the hard problem, and it is false because people feel pain. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-354](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-354.md)); worth reading as the statement of the meta-problem, explaining in topic-neutral terms why we judge that consciousness poses a hard problem, and as a survey of thirteen candidate mechanisms. Cite it for four things: the meta-problem as an "easy" problem with a research programme; the meta-problem challenge to theories of consciousness, which tells against IIT and biological theories; the analysis of debunking and coincidence arguments for illusionism; and the argument that only strong illusionism dissolves the hard problem, with a Moorean rejection of strong illusionism. Its own preferred solution is offered as "closer to a fleshed-out explanandum" than an explanation. |
| [LIT-426](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-426.md) | Macrocognition: A Theory of Distributed Minds and Collective Intentionality | Huebner (2014), DOI-10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199926275.001.0001. Per its publisher, the book argues that genuine cognition requires flexible goal-directed behaviour, which requires specialised representational systems integrated so as to cope fluidly with the environment, and so that collective mentality "should be posited where and only where specialized subroutines are integrated to yield goal-directed behavior that is sensitive to the concerns that are relevant to a group as such". On this view there are many kinds of collective minds, some more like honeybees or cats than people, and groups are unlikely to be full "believers". Unread: filed from the description and contents only. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and table of contents; no lawful full text was reachable (Oxford Academic is paywalled, the Internet Archive copy is lending-only, and no author-posted draft was found), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. Of the four works filed for the Minsky–Schwitzgebel bridge it is the one whose criterion for a collective mind is itself a decomposition criterion: mentality wherever specialised subroutines are integrated into goal-directed behaviour sensitive to the group's concerns. A close reading is the most likely of the four to change the bridge. |
| [LIT-427](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-427.md) | Pandemonium: A Paradigm for Learning | Selfridge (1959), Mechanisation of Thought Processes Vol. I (HMSO), pp. 513–526 plus discussion to p. 531. Pattern recognition by a "pandemonium": data demons hold the input, computational subdemons compute features, each cognitive demon "shrieks" a weighted sum of them, and a decision demon picks the loudest. The system learns by hill-climbing on the weights and by "natural selection" on the subdemons, culling those of low worth and breeding new ones by mutation and by "conjugation" of pairs. It is applied to telling dots from dashes in hand-keyed Morse. In the discussion McCarthy proposes reading the demons' private computation as unconscious and their public shouting as conscious thought. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-360](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-360.md)); worth reading as the first published architecture of a mind-like process built from many quasi-independent "demons", each doing one narrow job, with no part holding the whole's competence. That is the decomposition template that Minsky's agents inherit. Cite it as an engineering proposal with a preliminary result reported only in discussion, not as a theory of mind. Its one remark on consciousness is McCarthy's, in the discussion, and it is an aside. |
| [LIT-428](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-428.md) | Fluid Concepts and Creative Analogies: Computer Models of the Fundamental Mechanisms of Thought | Hofstadter & the Fluid Analogies Research Group (1995), Basic Books. The group's programme gathered in one volume: models of perception-driven analogy-making in microdomains (Seek-Whence, Jumbo, Numbo, Copycat, Tabletop, Letter Spirit, and the proposed Metacat), each chapter with a preface by Hofstadter, plus a critique of AI methodology and of how AI research is evaluated. Its contemporary reviewer in AI Magazine names two ideas under it: cognition as high-level perception, and the parallel terraced scan, by which coherent structure emerges from many probabilistic codelets without top-level control. | [LIT-429](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-429.md) | The Society of Mind | Minsky (1986), Simon & Schuster. The book-length statement of the Society of Mind programme, begun with Seymour Papert in the early 1970s. A mind is a society of many small agents, each mindless by itself, and intelligence comes from their diversity and organisation, not from one principle. The publisher presents it as a puzzle of self-contained one-page pieces that assemble into a theory. | [LIT-430](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-430.md) | The Intentional Stance | Dennett (1987), MIT Press. Per its publisher, the "first full-scale presentation of a theory of intentionality" Dennett had been developing for almost twenty years: we understand each other by adopting a stance, "a predictive strategy of interpretation that presupposes the rationality" of whatever we predict. Six chapters reprint papers of the 1980s, each followed by a new "Reflections" essay; the first and the last three chapters are new. Chapter 2 is True Believers ([LIT-398](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-398.md)).
