| [LIT-550](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-550.md) | Emotion and Adaptation | Lazarus (1991), Emotion and Adaptation, Oxford University Press, New York (ISBN 0-19-506994-3). The book-length statement of Lazarus's cognitive-motivational-relational appraisal theory; its chapter titles frame emotion through the person–environment relationship, motivation, coping and goal congruence. Eleven chapters run from definition and measurement through motivation and coping, cognition, causality, negative, positive and problematic emotions, development, social influence and health, to research, assessment, treatment and prevention. Unread. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 from Crossref's chapter records, not read, and no substitute was read either. The book (Oxford University Press, about 560 pages) is closed at the publisher. The shorter work by the same author that states the same theory, Lazarus (1991), "Progress on a cognitive-motivational-relational theory of emotion" (American Psychologist 46(8):819–834, DOI 10.1037/0003-066X.46.8.819), has no lawful open copy. APA does not make it free, and Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar list none. The only full text the web search found is in a bulk upload of Lazarus's journal articles to the Internet Archive by a private user, which is not a lawful source, so I did not open it. Other Lazarus emotion papers (American Psychologist 1991 46(4); Smith & Lazarus 1993; Psychological Inquiry 1995; Journal of Personality 2006) are also closed. His 1993 Annual Review of Psychology chapter is listed as free at the publisher, but annualreviews.org answered with a bot challenge. A human with library access could read the 1991 American Psychologist paper and file it as the read substitute. |
| [LIT-553](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-553.md) | Psychological Flexibility as a Fundamental Aspect of Health | Kashdan & Rottenberg (2010), Clinical Psychology Review 30(7):865–878. Psychological health is not a ratio of positive to negative experience or a set of fixed strengths but flexibility: adapting regulation to the situation, balancing time perspectives and life domains, and acting on values while open to experience. Inflexibility marks depression (rumination, emotion context insensitivity) and anxiety (experiential avoidance), and cardiac vagal control is proposed as an integrating marker. Executive functioning, default states and personality underlie it, and dynamic measurement is needed. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-436](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-436.md)), in the NIH author manuscript on PubMed Central; worth reading as the review that took "psychological flexibility" out of the ACT literature and made it a general construct of health. Flexibility is adapting to situational demands, reconfiguring mental resources, shifting perspective and balancing competing desires and life domains. Its absence (rumination, emotion context insensitivity, experiential avoidance, low cardiac vagal control) runs through depression and anxiety. Executive functioning, default mental states and personality are its "building blocks". It is a narrative synthesis: no meta-analysis of its own, the causal direction between inflexibility and disorder is left open by its own account, and it asks for dynamic measures in place of the global self-reports the ACT line relies on. |
| [LIT-554](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-554.md) | The Emerging Field of Emotion Regulation: An Integrative Review | Gross (1998), Review of General Psychology 2(3):271–299. Emotions are response tendencies (behavioural, experiential, physiological) called forth by evaluated situations and open to modulation. Emotion regulation is how people influence which emotions they have, when, and how they are experienced and expressed, and it is distinct from coping, mood regulation and defense. A process model places regulation at five points in emotion generation: situation selection, situation modification, attentional deployment, cognitive change (reappraisal), and response modulation (suppression). The first four are antecedent-focused, the last response-focused. Dysregulation is said to figure in over half of the DSM-IV Axis I disorders and all of Axis II. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-429](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-429.md)); worth reading as the founding statement of the process model of emotion regulation, the five-family scheme (situation selection, situation modification, attentional deployment, cognitive change, response modulation) that later regulation research and many therapies are organised around. It defines emotion regulation as "the processes by which individuals influence which emotions they have, when they have them, and how they experience and express these emotions" (p. 275) and separates it from coping, mood regulation and defense. It is a conceptual review: no data of its own, and it says the scheme is "a set of working distinctions" (p. 282). |
| [LIT-555](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-555.md) | Acceptance and Commitment Therapy: Model, Processes and Outcomes | Hayes, Luoma, Bond, Masuda & Lillis (2006), Behaviour Research and Therapy 44(1):1–25. The ACT model: psychopathology is psychological inflexibility, produced when language (cognitive fusion) and experiential avoidance dominate direct contingencies, and ACT restores flexibility through six processes. A review of correlational, component, mediational and outcome studies finds the model "broadly supportive" but the literature immature, and the evidence suggests ACT works through different processes from traditional CBT. Read in an early author manuscript whose numbers differ from the published paper's. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-431](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-431.md)), but in an early manuscript, not the published text; worth reading as the canonical statement of the ACT model of psychopathology, "psychological inflexibility", and of the six processes ACT targets. Cognitive fusion and experiential avoidance (from [LIT-551](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-551.md)) narrow behaviour, and acceptance, defusion, present-moment contact, self as context, values and committed action restore flexibility. The copy read is an author manuscript in Georgia State University's repository that still carries "xx" placeholders, and its numbers differ from the published paper's as Kashdan and Rottenberg report them (21 studies against 32; an AAQ correlation printed ".030" against ".42"). Use its model and argument, not its numbers. Its own verdict on the evidence is "broadly supportive" but "not mature". |
| [LIT-563](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-563.md) | HDDM: Hierarchical Bayesian Estimation of the Drift-Diffusion Model in Python | Wiecki, Sofer & Frank (2013), Frontiers in Neuroinformatics 7:14. HDDM is an open-source Python package that estimates the drift diffusion model (and the linear ballistic accumulator) by hierarchical Bayesian MCMC: subject parameters drawn from group distributions with informative priors, full posteriors, outlier handling, and regression of parameters on trial-by-trial covariates. A tutorial reproduces a theta-power effect on decision threshold that reverses under subthalamic deep brain stimulation. In simulations hierarchical Bayes recovers parameters and detects effects better than χ²-quantile and maximum-likelihood fitting, most with few trials. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-466](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-466.md)); worth reading as the methods paper for HDDM, the Python package that fits the drift diffusion model by hierarchical Bayesian estimation (PyMC, MCMC), with subject parameters drawn from group distributions and trial-by-trial regressions of parameters on covariates such as EEG power. Its simulations show hierarchical Bayes recovering parameters with less error than per-subject χ²-quantile, maximum-likelihood or non-hierarchical Bayesian fits, most of all with few trials, and detecting drift-rate differences and covariate effects more often. The comparisons are the authors' own, on data simulated from the model being fitted, and its hypothesis tests on the group posterior differ from the t-tests used for the other methods. |
| [LIT-565](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-565.md) | The Time Course of Perceptual Choice: The Leaky, Competing Accumulator Model | Usher & McClelland (2001), Psychological Review 108(3):550–592. Perceptual choice as gradual, stochastic accumulation in one unit per alternative, with leakage and lateral inhibition between units and a threshold at zero. For two choices the linearised difference is an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process with net leak K = k − β; K = 0 recovers the classical diffusion model, and K ≠ 0 bounds asymptotic accuracy. The model fits time–accuracy curves slightly better than diffusion with drift variance, fits Vickers's latency–discriminability data, predicts individual primacy or recency biases confirmed in a new experiment, and yields Hick's law under a constant-accuracy criterion. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-449](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-449.md)); worth reading as the source of the leaky, competing accumulator (LCA): one leaky accumulator per alternative, lateral inhibition between them, a threshold-linear floor at zero, and an absolute response criterion. In the linear two-choice case the difference between accumulators is an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process with net leak K = k − β, so the classical diffusion model is the special case K = 0 and accuracy given unlimited time is bounded whenever K ≠ 0. Its evidence for leakage over drift variance is a modest likelihood advantage on 3 participants (combined ratio about 62 to 1, 7 of 9 curves), and the authors concede that a diffusion model with drift variance, starting-point variance and decision boundaries is hard to tell apart from it. |
| [LIT-566](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-566.md) | Defining Agency: Individuality, Normativity, Asymmetry, and Spatio-temporality in Action | Barandiaran, Di Paolo & Rohde (2009), Adaptive Behavior 17(5):367–386. Three conditions are jointly necessary and sufficient for minimal agency: the system defines its own individuality, it is the active source of modulations of its coupling with the environment (interactional asymmetry), and it regulates that coupling by norms it generates (normativity). Generatively, an agent is an open autonomous system (a precarious network of mutually enabling processes) that adaptively modulates its coupling so as to maintain some of its constituent processes. Minimal life satisfies this; life is sufficient for agency but not necessary. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-458](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-458.md)), from the authors' own deposit of the accepted text. Worth reading as the standard organizational definition of minimal agency, and as the clearest statement that an agent is not the same thing as an individual. Individuality is one of three conditions, with interactional asymmetry and normativity; it is a precondition for the other two and is not sufficient for agency. The generative definition: an agent is an autonomous organization that adaptively regulates its coupling with its environment and contributes to sustaining itself as a consequence. The paper rejects statistical and energetic measures of asymmetry as sufficient, and says systems optimising an externally fixed function should not be treated as models of agency. |
| [LIT-568](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-568.md) | Précis: Being No One | Metzinger (2005), PSYCHE 11(5), the author's précis of Being No One. Minimal consciousness is a global world-model in a window of presence that cannot be recognised as a model (globality, presentationality, transparency). A phenomenal self is a transparent self-model: "no such things as selves exist in the world". Transparency comes in degrees, and the self-model's opaque partition is what lets humans doubt their own self-representation. The unity of consciousness is a single global functional cluster. A first-person perspective is a phenomenal model of the intentionality relation, and iterating it yields introspective and social intelligence. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-460](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-460.md)), as the read substitute for Being No One ([LIT-467](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-467.md)), which it summarises in Metzinger's own words. Worth reading as the most complete short statement of the self-model theory of subjectivity (SMT): more of the machinery than "Self models" ([LIT-450](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-450.md)), in particular the six constraints, the degrees of transparency, and the phenomenal model of the intentionality relation (PMIR). Phenomenal selfhood is a transparent self-model, "a function realized by a lack of information"; "no such things as selves exist in the world". The unity of a conscious world is a global functional cluster bound by "highest-order binding". It states the theory and its predictions; the evidence is cited, not shown, and the neural sections say how little is known. |
| [LIT-569](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-569.md) | The Physics of Optimal Decision Making: A Formal Analysis of Models of Performance in Two-Alternative Forced-Choice Tasks | Bogacz, Brown, Moehlis, Holmes & Cohen (2006), Psychological Review 113(4):700–765. The pure drift diffusion model implements the SPRT and Neyman–Pearson test, so it is the optimal two-choice decision process. The O-U, mutual inhibition (Usher–McClelland), feedforward inhibition and pooled inhibition (Wang) models reduce to it for balanced parameters; the race model does not. For reward rate, Bayes risk and two accuracy-weighted criteria there is a unique optimal threshold, giving parameter-free optimal performance curves. With biased priors the optimal starting point is proportional to the log prior odds. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-461](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-461.md)), main text and Appendix B in full, Appendix A (the derivations) by section only; worth reading as the paper that puts the two-choice decision models in one frame and ties them to the sequential probability ratio test. The pure drift diffusion model is the continuum limit of the SPRT, so it is the fastest for a given accuracy and the most accurate for a given time. Of six models, all but the race model reduce to it in some parameter range: the Usher–McClelland mutual inhibition model when leak equals inhibition and both are large, the feedforward inhibition model when its inhibitory and excitatory weights are equal. Each reward criterion has a unique optimal threshold, which gives testable optimal performance curves. The optimality results hold for the pure model with stationary evidence and two alternatives. |
| [LIT-571](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-571.md) | Participatory sense-making: An enactive approach to social cognition | De Jaegher & Di Paolo (2007), Phenomenology and the Cognitive Sciences 6(4):485–507. Coordination between coupled systems is cheap and common. When patterns of coordination and the course of an encounter shape each other, the interaction acquires its own operationally closed, precarious organization. Social interaction is then regulated coupling between autonomous agents that constitutes an autonomous relational organization without destroying the agents' autonomy. Because sense-making is embodied in movement, interactors can coordinate their sense-making, along a spectrum from modulated individual sense-making to jointly created meaning. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-456](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-456.md)), from the published version posted on De Jaegher's own site. Worth reading as the founding statement of participatory sense-making. A social interaction is defined as regulated coupling between autonomous agents that itself becomes an autonomous organization in the relational domain, without destroying the agents' autonomy; coordinating sense-making in interaction can generate meanings neither individual had. The argument is conceptual, illustrated by everyday cases and by the perceptual-crossing experiments; nothing is measured in the paper. |
| [LIT-576](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-576.md) | The Diffusion Decision Model: Theory and Data for Two-Choice Decision Tasks | Ratcliff & McKoon (2008), Neural Computation 20(4):873–922. A review of the diffusion decision model for fast two-choice tasks, with three new motion-discrimination experiments. Noisy evidence accumulates from a starting point z to one of two boundaries (0, a) at drift v, plus non-decision time and across-trial variability in v, z and Ter. The model fits accuracy and full correct and error RT distributions, and maps difficulty to drift, speed–accuracy instructions to boundary separation and stimulus proportion mainly to starting point. Applications cover aging, aphasia and links to neural firing. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-445](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-445.md)), from the author manuscript in PubMed Central; worth reading as the canonical statement of the diffusion decision model and of what it is for. Two-choice RT and accuracy are decomposed into drift rate (quality of evidence), boundary separation (caution), starting point (bias) and non-decision time, plus across-trial variability in drift, starting point and non-decision time. Three new motion-discrimination experiments show each manipulation landing on its own parameter: difficulty on drift, speed–accuracy instructions on boundaries, stimulus proportion mainly on starting point. Its closing claim, that diffusion models have come "as near to provid[ing] a solution to simple decision making as is possible in behavioral science", is the authors' assessment, not a result. |
| [LIT-578](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-578.md) | Dynamic Patterns: The Self-Organization of Brain and Behavior | Kelso (1995), Dynamic Patterns: The Self-Organization of Brain and Behavior, MIT Press, xvii + 334 pp. The book-length statement of coordination dynamics. Unread: registered from catalogue records. What the record knows of its content comes from the works that cite it: the coordination potential of the HKB model (reproduced in Kelso 2021, Box 1), absolute versus relative coordination (De Jaegher & Di Paolo 2007, citing p. 98), a chapter on how HKB arose (ch. 3) and one on brain rhythms (ch. 8), per Kelso 2021. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 as a seed, not read. No lawful full text was found: the book has no DOI, is not listed as open access, and MIT Press's page refused an automated request. Under the owner's rule for books it is supplanted by a shorter work by the same author, Kelso's 2021 retrospective on the HKB model ([LIT-601](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-601.md)), which was read. It is filed because it is the citation others reach for when they mean coordination dynamics, relative coordination or metastability; De Jaegher & Di Paolo ([LIT-571](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-571.md)) and Raja et al. ([LIT-598](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-598.md)) both cite it. |
| [LIT-580](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-580.md) | Uncertainty-based competition between prefrontal and dorsolateral striatal systems for behavioral control | Daw, Niv & Dayan (2005), Nature Neuroscience 8(12):1704-1711. Habitual and goal-directed control are model-free ("caching") and model-based ("tree-search") reinforcement learners in dorsolateral striatum and prefrontal cortex. Behaviour follows whichever controller's value estimate is less uncertain under approximate Bayesian versions of each. Simulations reproduce the devaluation data: over-training yields devaluation-insensitive habit, except for actions near reward or in tasks with more actions and outcomes. Both controllers serve the same ends; neither is the "irrational" one. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-459](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-459.md)), supplementary methods not read. Worth reading as the founding statement of model-based versus model-free control as two brain systems, and of arbitration between them by relative uncertainty. Goal-directed (devaluation-sensitive) behaviour is a prefrontal "tree-search" controller, statistically efficient but noisy to compute. Habit is a dorsolateral-striatal "caching" controller, cheap but data-hungry and blind to revaluation. Each controls behaviour when its value estimate is the more certain, which reproduces why over-training produces habits unless the task is complex or the action near the reward. Both controllers pursue "identical rational ends": a rejection of the impulsive-limbic-versus-rational-prefrontal picture. |
| [LIT-581](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-581.md) | Hierarchically organized behavior and its neural foundations: A reinforcement learning perspective | Botvinick, Niv & Barto (2009), Cognition 113(3):262-280. Hierarchical RL groups actions into reusable "options" with their own policies, subgoals and pseudo-reward. That eases the scaling problem by cutting the number of decisions to explore and learn. The paper builds an actor-critic version and maps option identifiers to DLPFC, option-specific policies to dorsolateral striatum, and option-specific values and option-length prediction errors to OFC. Unsuitable options produce negative transfer, so how useful options are discovered is the central open problem. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-451](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-451.md)), from the PubMed Central author manuscript; the online appendix with the equations was not read. Worth reading as the bridge between hierarchical reinforcement learning (temporally abstract "options") and the psychology and neuroscience of hierarchically organized behaviour. Options ease the scaling problem of RL by shrinking search and learning to a few decision points. An actor-critic version maps option identifiers to dorsolateral PFC, option-specific policies to dorsolateral striatum, and option-specific values and extended prediction errors to orbitofrontal cortex. The problem it puts first is option discovery: the wrong options cause negative transfer, as in human problem solving. |
| [LIT-584](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-584.md) | Model-based and model-free Pavlovian reward learning: Revaluation, revision, and revelation | Dayan & Berridge (2014), Cognitive, Affective, & Behavioral Neuroscience 14(2):473-492. Pavlovian prediction is not only model-free. A cue that had predicted disgusting salt became instantly "wanted" when a never-experienced salt appetite was induced, before the salt was retasted, which needs a prediction of the outcome's identity revalued against the current bodily state. Over-training may "defocus" outcome representations rather than hand control to a model-free system. Dopamine may carry model-based evaluations. No algorithm for the revaluation is given. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-463](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-463.md)), from the PubMed Central author manuscript. Worth reading as the argument that Pavlovian prediction, usually modelled as purely model-free, is also model-based. In the "Dead Sea salt" experiment a lever that had predicted a disgusting salt solution became, on first presentation after a novel sodium appetite was induced and before any salt was retasted, nearly as attractive as a sucrose lever, with mesolimbic activation. A cached value cannot do that. The CS must predict the outcome's identity, and its value must be recomputed against the current bodily state. The paper adds "defocusing" of outcome representations as a model-based route to apparent habit, and argues that dopamine can carry model-based evaluations. |
| [LIT-585](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-585.md) | The Expected Value of Control: An Integrative Theory of Anterior Cingulate Cortex Function | Shenhav, Botvinick & Cohen (2013), Neuron 79(2):217-240. Control is allocated by a cost-benefit decision. The expected value of control (EVC) of a candidate control signal is its probability-weighted payoff, with future value discounted, minus an intrinsic cost rising with its intensity. dACC monitors state and outcome information and specifies the identity and intensity of the EVC-maximizing signal. Lateral PFC and subcortical structures implement it. The account integrates conflict monitoring, effort costs and the override of defaults (exploration, foraging, patience). | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-446](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-446.md)), from the PubMed Central author manuscript. Worth reading as the standard statement that cognitive control is allocated by a cost-benefit decision. The "expected value of control" (EVC) of a control signal, which has an identity (which task) and an intensity (how much), is its expected payoff minus an intrinsic cost that rises with intensity. Dorsal anterior cingulate cortex is proposed to monitor and to specify the EVC-maximizing signal, which lateral PFC and subcortical structures then implement. It is a review and synthesis: the model is stated, not fitted, and the authors say the ingredients are not new. |
| [LIT-595](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-595.md) | “First we invented stories, then they changed us”: The Evolution of Narrative Identity | McAdams (2019), Evolutionary Studies in Imaginative Culture 3(1):1–18. Narrative identity is "the internalized and evolving story a person invents to explain how he or she has become the person he or she is becoming", giving a life "unity, moral purpose, and temporal coherence". Storytelling evolved with human hypersociality. The self develops from social actor (by age 2) to motivated agent (school years) to autobiographical author (adolescence). Agentic and redemptive stories go with well-being and generativity, and cultures supply master narratives. "Biology guides and culture fills in the details." | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-470](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-470.md)), as the read substitute for McAdams & McLean, "Narrative Identity" (2013; [LIT-572](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-572.md)), which has no lawful copy and whose definition this essay takes over word for word. Worth reading as McAdams's own short statement of narrative identity: "the internalized and evolving story a person invents to explain how he or she has become the person he or she is becoming", which gives a life "unity, moral purpose, and temporal coherence". It places the life story as the third layer of a self that develops from actor to agent to author, and reports that story features (agency, redemption, coherence) predict well-being and generativity. A review essay: the empirical claims are cited, not shown, and the evolutionary story is offered as plausible, not tested. |
| [LIT-598](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-598.md) | The Markov blanket trick: On the scope of the free energy principle and active inference | Raja, Valluri, Baggs, Chemero & Anderson (2021), Physics of Life Reviews 39:49–72. Restating the FEP's derivation (Langevin dynamics, NESS, Helmholtz decomposition, Markov blanket, variational bound), the authors grant that it is true of things so defined. But blankets apply to every "thing", not everything (the candle flame is excluded); the partition is placed by modelling convenience; relational properties (heading, affordances) and constitutive self-organization (a membrane the cell makes) fall outside it. The blanket's real role is to supply the partition variational Bayes needs. Active inference presupposes perception and action in its generative models. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-450](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-450.md)), from the authors' PhilSci-Archive preprint (March 2021); the Physics of Life Reviews version was not seen. Worth reading as the scope critique of the free energy principle: granted its premises the principle is true, but it applies only to "things" already given a Markov-blanket partition, the partition is placed where the model needs it, and relational properties and constitutive self-organization fall outside it. The blanket is a "trick" that lets any thing be modelled as a variational autoencoder. Active inference, as a process theory, presupposes perception and action in the generative model it is handed. |
| [LIT-600](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-600.md) | Attention to Action: Willed and Automatic Control of Behavior | Norman & Shallice (1986), in Davidson, Schwartz & Shapiro (eds.), Consciousness and Self-Regulation vol. 4 (Plenum), pp. 1-18; first issued as CHIP Report 99 (UCSD, December 1980). Per the report's ERIC abstract: routine action runs off by "contention scheduling" among competing schemas, and a "supervisory attentional mechanism" biases that selection for novel, ill-learned, dangerous or planned action; "will becomes the application of attentional resources to the control of action". Unread. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 from bibliographic records and from the ERIC abstract of the 1980 technical report, not read. The 1986 chapter is not open access: Unpaywall reports no open copy, and SpringerLink returned a JavaScript bot challenge, which was not pursued. The 1980 version (CHIP Report 99, University of California San Diego, catalogued by ERIC as ED205562, "Technical Report No. 8006", 43 pages) was the brief's lead. ERIC has a catalogue record and abstract but no full text: its fulltext URL returns 404. The copies on Academia.edu sit behind a bot challenge, and those on ResearchGate and Scribd are uploads this record does not use. No DTIC copy was found. A human could ask UCSD's library or the authors' institutions for the CHIP report, or read the chapter through a library, and move this to Active. |
| [LIT-601](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-601.md) | The Haken–Kelso–Bunz (HKB) model: from matter to movement to mind | Kelso (2021), Biological Cybernetics 115(4):305–322, a 60th-anniversary retrospective. HKB models bimanual coordination by the relative phase φ, with dφ/dt = −a sin φ − 2b sin 2φ and potential V = −a cos φ − b cos 2φ: both in-phase and anti-phase are stable for b/a > 1/4, and anti-phase loses stability below it, as observed when movement frequency rises. Noise, symmetry breaking (Δω) and metastability extend it; with Kuramoto's model it becomes a generalized HKB for many agents. The same dynamics is reported within a body, between people and with machines, and in brain activity. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-467](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-467.md)), from the free-to-read publisher PDF. Filed in place of Kelso's book Dynamic Patterns ([LIT-578](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-578.md)) and as the read account of the paywalled Haken–Kelso–Bunz paper ([LIT-588](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-588.md)), both Deferred. Worth reading as Kelso's own short statement of coordination dynamics: the HKB order-parameter equation for relative phase, its stochastic and symmetry-breaking extensions, metastability as relative coordination, the generalized HKB–Kuramoto model, and the claim that one coordination dynamics holds within and between people. It is a retrospective by an author of the model, not a review, and it says so. |
| [LIT-603](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-603.md) | The Emperor's New Markov Blankets | Bruineberg, Dołęga, Dewhurst & Baltieri (2020 preprint; BBS 45:e183, 2022). Markov blankets entered variational inference as Pearl's conditional-independence shields, tools on a scientist's map. In the free-energy literature since Friston 2013 they became boundaries in the world between agent and environment: "Friston blankets". The two are different constructs; Friston blankets need extra assumptions (a chosen internal node, sensorimotor labels, steady state, sparse coupling) that the formalism does not supply. Using them for metaphysical conclusions ("inference within a model") requires metaphysical premises; used instrumentally ("inference with a model") they are innocent but philosophically idle. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-447](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-447.md)), but in its December 2020 PhilSci-Archive version; the Behavioral and Brain Sciences target article of 2021–2022 is, by the authors' own note, "heavily rewritten" and could not be read lawfully beyond its abstract. Worth reading as the critique that names the problem: "Pearl blankets", the conditional-independence tool of graphical models, are conflated with "Friston blankets", a realist construct meant to be the boundary between an agent and its world. The second cannot be read off the mathematics of the first, and its use to settle questions about life and mind needs metaphysical premises of its own. It re-runs the primordial-soup simulation of [LIT-526](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-526.md) and shows how the blanket found there depends on modelling choices. |
| [LIT-606](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-606.md) | Thine Own Self: True Self-Concept Accessibility and Meaning in Life | Schlegel, Hicks, Arndt & King (2009), JPSP 96(2):473–490. Five studies: faster "me" judgments for one's own true-self traits (residualized on speed for control traits) predict presence of meaning in life, while actual-self accessibility does not, controlling affect, need satisfaction and (Study 4) AI-3 authenticity, which was itself uncorrelated with true-self accessibility. Subliminal priming of true-self traits raised reported meaning (Studies 3 and 5), for disliked traits as much as liked ones. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-469](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-469.md)); worth reading as the experimental case that the true self-concept, as distinct from self-reported authenticity, matters to felt meaning. In five student studies (N = 56 to 149), how quickly people classify their own "true self" traits predicts presence of meaning in life over and above actual-self accessibility, need satisfaction and AI-3 authenticity, and subliminally priming true-self traits raises reported meaning, even when the traits are disliked. Effects are small, meaning is self-report only, and the Study 5 interaction is printed with an F that cannot carry its stated p. |
| [LIT-615](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-615.md) | An Active Inference Approach to Modeling Structure Learning: Concept Learning as an Example Case | Smith, Schwartenbeck, Parr & Friston (2020), Front. Comput. Neurosci. 14:41. A partially observed Markov decision process with eight animal "slots", some starting with flat likelihoods, learns new concepts without feedback: a slot is engaged only when its flat mapping explains a feature combination better than any learned concept. Bayesian model reduction on the learned prior over states then resets slots the data did not need. In 100 runs per condition the true number of concepts won in 45–80% of runs for 4–7 concepts and rarely for 2–3, and in every run when the likelihood was given. The agent also generalises to an unseen animal in one shot, and the paper simulates neural and dopaminergic responses. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-485](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-485.md)); worth reading as the record's worked example of structure learning in an active-inference agent: "model expansion" by spare hidden-state slots whose flat likelihoods win inference only for a truly novel stimulus, and "model reduction" by applying Bayesian model reduction to the agent's learned prior over states, so that unused slots are reset. It is a proof of concept with eight animals and six features. Reduction recovered the true number of concepts in 45–80% of 100 runs for 4–7 concepts, failed for 2–3, and succeeded every time only when the likelihood mapping was given rather than learned. |
| [LIT-625](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-625.md) | Functional Role and Truth Conditions | Block (1987), Aristotelian Society Supplementary Volume 61:157–181, the first paper of a symposium with John Campbell. Functional role semantics can explain five facts about concepts (holism of concepts and thoughts, incommensurability, limits on attributing irrationality, structure). To give Twin Earth truth conditions, a private-use theory must add a referential factor; a public-use theory must extend roles into the world with devices from the theory of reference (dominant causal source, borrowed reference, experts). Either way the result is equivalent to a two-factor theory whose internal factor is narrow meaning. Burge's arthritis cases need, in addition, functional role in a language with its structure of deference. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-492](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-492.md)); worth reading as the work the record cites as "Block 1987" ([NOTE-117](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-117.md), after Drayson): a short argument that any use theory of meaning that gets Twin Earth truth conditions right, whether it starts from private use in thought or public use in communication, ends up equivalent to a two-factor theory with a narrow, in-the-head functional role and a referential factor. It leaves room for narrow content without arguing for it, and its appendix concedes that Burge's arthritis cases need functional role in a language, structured by deference, as well as in the individual. Block says outright that he has not tried to settle whether narrow content is explanatory. |
| [LIT-626](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-626.md) | Three types of phenomenal consciousness and their functional roles: unfolding the ALARM theory of consciousness | Newen & Montemayor (2025), Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 380:20240314. The ALARM theory: phenomenal consciousness has two levels of experience and three functions. Basic arousal, realisable without cortex, alarms the body when a homeostatic variable leaves its tolerance range, overriding slow regulation with no choice involved; it adds lasting care for the injury and one-shot, generalised avoidance learning. General alertness, cortical and attention-guided, enables flexible learning and decision-making. Reflexive self-consciousness is general alertness with metacognitive self-relational content, not a third kind of experience, and enables long-term planning that accounts for one's own and others' mindsets. IIT, higher-order theories and GNWT are faulted for tying consciousness to neocortex and leaving basic arousal out. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-489](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-489.md)); worth reading as the shortest statement of the ALARM theory: phenomenal consciousness has two levels of experience, basic arousal (subcortical, an alarm that overrides slow homeostatic regulation) and general alertness (cortical, attention-guided, for flexible learning and choice), plus reflexive self-consciousness, which is general alertness with metacognitive self-relational content and its own function, long-term planning. Its evidence is a short list of cited findings (hydranencephaly, decorticate cats, central lateral thalamus stimulation in macaques), and the functional claims are argued, not tested. |
| [LIT-629](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-629.md) | Two neural correlates of consciousness | Block (2005), Trends in Cognitive Sciences 9(2):46–52. There are at least two neural correlates of consciousness: a phenomenal NCC, the minimal basis of an experience's content (recurrent activation of MT/V5 with V1 for seen motion), and an access NCC, frontoparietal activation that broadcasts the content in a global workspace. Because access is a winner-take-all competition, a recurrent sensory representation can lose and stay unaccessed. Signal-detection analyses of exclusion tasks and of V1 figure–ground modulation in monkeys suggest experience without access. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-496](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-496.md)); worth reading as the short empirical turn of Block's distinction: a phenomenal NCC (recurrent activity in sensory areas, such as MT/V5 with V1 for seen motion) and an access NCC (frontoparietal broadcasting), with a winner-take-all contest for access as the reason the first can occur without the second. Its evidence is signal-detection reasoning: Supèr et al.'s V1 figure–ground modulation persists when low salience or many catch trials uncouple it from the monkey's saccade. The case is suggestive, "a glimmer", and the later papers make it at length. |
| [LIT-630](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-630.md) | The Mind as the Software of the Brain | Block (1995), in Smith & Osherson (eds.), An Invitation to Cognitive Science, 2nd ed., vol. 3, Thinking, MIT Press, ch. 11, pp. 377–425. The computer model explains intelligence by decomposing it into ever stupider processors that bottom out in primitive processors, the only devices for which behaviourism is true. The brain is a syntactic engine driving a semantic engine, by an isomorphism between symbol transitions and rational relations among meanings, which must hold counterfactually, so a wall is not every computer. Intentionality comes from the language of thought plus functional role semantics. Stich's syntactic theory falls to the "Reductionist Cruncher", and the systems reply answers Searle, though Block doubts the Chinese system is phenomenally conscious. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-490](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-490.md)); worth reading as Block's textbook statement of what "the mind is the software of the brain" means: intelligence explained by functional decomposition into primitive processors, the brain as a syntactic engine driving a semantic engine, intentionality explained by the language of thought plus functional role semantics, and the defence of that picture against Dennett's objections, Stich's syntactic theory (by the "Reductionist Cruncher") and Searle's Chinese room. It is a survey for an introductory volume, so its arguments are compressed, but it states clearly two things the record uses: intelligence is future-oriented and intentionality past-oriented, and the computer model may give intentionality without phenomenal consciousness. |
| [LIT-631](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-631.md) | Conscious Processing and the Global Neuronal Workspace Hypothesis | Mashour, Roelfsema, Changeux & Dehaene (2020), Neuron 105(5):776–798. A review of the global neuronal workspace hypothesis by its proponents. Conscious access is a sudden, non-linear ignition of a distributed network of long-range pyramidal neurons, with prefrontal cortex a key hub, that amplifies, sustains and broadcasts one representation; unseen stimuli produce only a decaying wave. Evidence: a late (>200–300 ms) divergence between seen and unseen trials across modalities, prefrontal ignition in monkeys tied to the signal-detection threshold, and the disconnection of frontal-parietal networks by every major class of anaesthetic. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-510](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-510.md)); worth reading as the record's first source statement of the global neuronal workspace (GNW): conscious access is a non-linear "ignition" in which recurrent loops among long-range prefrontal, parietal and other hub neurons amplify, sustain and broadcast one representation to the brain's specialised processors. Its strongest evidence is van Vugt et al.'s (2018) monkey recordings, where seen and unseen stimuli both drive V1 and V4 but only seen ones (and false alarms) ignite sustained prefrontal firing, and the signal-detection threshold maps onto the ignition threshold. It is a review by the theory's proponents, explicitly a theory of access, and it concedes that the four leading theories cannot yet be told apart experimentally. |
| [LIT-632](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-632.md) | Comparing the Major Theories of Consciousness | Block (2009), in Gazzaniga (ed.), The Cognitive Neurosciences, 4th ed., MIT Press, ch. 77, pp. 1111–1122. Compares the three theories neuroscientists take most seriously: higher-order thought, the global workspace and the biological theory. Only the biological theory fully acknowledges the explanatory gap; the others replace it with a puzzle their own theory creates. Concept dualism stops the gap becoming dualism. The ambitious higher-order theory also fails on stipulation, mismatch and infants. Integrated information is criticised as a theory of intelligence. The biological theory is the least friendly to machine consciousness. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-505](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-505.md)); worth reading as Block's comparison of the higher-order thought, global workspace and biological theories by one test: does the theory recognise the explanatory gap? The ambitious higher-order theory and the workspace theory turn the gap into a puzzle of their own making, so only the biological theory "fully acknowledges" it; concept dualism keeps that from becoming dualism. Also the source of the "biological theory" that Chalmers's meta-problem paper cites as "Block 2009", and a short argument that the biological theory is less friendly to machine consciousness than its rivals. |
| [LIT-633](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-633.md) | Cross-region neuron co-firing mediated by ripple oscillations supports distributed working memory representations | Verzhbinsky, Daume, Cheng, Rutishauser & Halgren (2026), Nature Neuroscience 29:2566–2577. In 1,373 single units from hippocampus, amygdala, vmPFC, ACC and preSMA of 35 epilepsy patients doing a Sternberg task, ripples (70–100 Hz) co-occur between bundles up to about 220 mm apart with no decline beyond the local bundle, and cross-region unit co-firing rises about 30% during co-ripples. That rise exceeds a rate-only null (STTC 117% higher), grows with memory load, and co-ripples hold more repetitions of a stimulus's encoding co-firing at retrieval, more on fast trials. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-494](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-494.md)); worth reading as single-unit evidence that brief co-occurring ~90 Hz ripples in distant human forebrain sites (up to about 220 mm, across hemispheres) mark windows of raised cross-region co-firing, about 30% above no-ripple periods and beyond what firing rates alone predict, that this scales with working-memory load, and that stimulus-specific co-firing from encoding recurs more often inside co-ripples at retrieval, most of all on fast trials. One reanalysed open dataset (35 patients, one Sternberg task, load 1 versus 3), clinically placed electrodes, and correlational throughout: nothing perturbs the ripples. |
| [LIT-634](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-634.md) | Inverted Earth | Block (1990), Philosophical Perspectives 4:53–79. Inverted Earth has complementary colours and inverted colour words, so a visitor with colour-inverting lenses notices nothing. After long residence, or for a twin raised there with a molecule-for-molecule identical brain, the intentional content of the experience of the sky inverts (it is about yellow) and so does its functional role in a long-arm description, while qualitative content stays the same. So qualitative content is not a functional state and the intentional/qualitative distinction stands. Public colour terms like "looks red" express intentional, not qualitative, content. A brain-internal functional theory of qualia would escape, but nobody has said what it is. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-504](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-504.md)); worth reading as the source of the Inverted Earth argument: a subject moved, unaware, to a planet of complementary colours and inverted colour words keeps the same qualitative content while, over time, the intentional content and the (long-arm) functional role of the experience invert. That is the converse of the inverted spectrum, and it needs no internal switch, so the subject's testimony is undisturbed and brain supervenience is on the qualia realist's side. It refutes functionalism about qualia only in its long-arm form; Block concedes a short-arm functional theory of qualia would sink it, and answers that only with a burden of proof. |
| [LIT-635](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-635.md) | Mental Paint | Block (2003), in Hahn & Ramberg (eds.), Reflections and Replies, MIT Press, pp. 165–200. Phenomenal character outruns representational content. Internalist representationism must find a functional difference for every phenomenal one, and Erisa, raised where colours keep changing, has vivid colour differences with no abiding functional ones. Against externalist representationism: a swampman has phenomenal character and no content; attention is not awareness, so transparency fails as a claim about awareness; on Inverted Earth what stays the same is mental paint; and normal variation in colour vision means, if representationism is true, that a standard chip cannot look its shade to both men and women. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-511](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-511.md)); worth reading as Block's fullest case against representationism about phenomenal character ("phenomenism" against "representationism"). It separates mental paint (phenomenal properties that represent) from mental oil (phenomenal properties that do not), argues against internalist representationism with Erisa, raised among colours that keep changing, and against externalist representationism with Inverted Earth, long-term memory, and an empirical "shifted spectra" argument from normal variation in cone sensitivity and in where people place unique green. Several of its arguments are offered as pressure, not proof, and Block says so. |
| [LIT-636](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-636.md) | The Border Between Seeing and Thinking | Block (2023), Oxford University Press, open access. Argues, by Block's own précis ([LIT-649](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-649.md)), that perception is constitutively iconic, nonconceptual and nonpropositional while cognition is paradigmatically discursive, conceptual and propositional, using scientific marks of perception such as adaptation; that core cognition splits between the two; and, in a chapter on consciousness, against cognitive theories of consciousness. Unread: seeded from the chapter list and the précis. | Deferred — seeded 2026-10-03 from Crossref's book and chapter records and from Block's own précis ([LIT-649](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-649.md)), not read. The book is open access at Oxford University Press under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (Unpaywall lists the OUP book PDF), so a lawful full text exists, but academic.oup.com answered every request with a Cloudflare "Just a moment..." challenge, and OAPEN and DOAB, which normally mirror such books, refused this session's requests; I did not try to get past either. The précis was read in its place. Filed because the record cites the book twice ([NOTE-104](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-104.md) for pp. 454–458 on the neural replacement argument, [NOTE-150](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-150.md) for the perception–cognition border), and those citations need a code. A human reader can open the OUP copy, and a reading would move this to Active. |
| [LIT-637](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-637.md) | What Is Wrong with the No-Report Paradigm and How to Fix It | Block (2019), Trends in Cognitive Sciences 23(12):1003–1013. Whether perceptual consciousness needs prefrontal circuits cannot be settled by no-report paradigms, because subjects not asked to report may still think about what they see, and that thought tracks the percept. A no-post-perceptual-cognition paradigm is needed. Brascamp et al.'s rivalry with inconspicuous switches is one, and it found no detectable prefrontal difference. Box 2 argues that binocular rivalry is driven by local features, against the predictive-processing account. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-495](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-495.md)); worth reading as the argument that removing report does not isolate the neural basis of conscious perception, because subjects, monkeys included, can still think about what they see ("the bored monkey problem"). What is needed is a paradigm with no post-perceptual cognition that differs between percepts. Brascamp et al.'s inconspicuous binocular rivalry, whose switches subjects could not tell from constant random changes, is offered as one, and found no prefrontal difference by fMRI. Block flags that fMRI may be too coarse, and that ECoG could still favour prefrontalism. |
| [LIT-638](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-638.md) | Interacting spiral wave patterns underlie complex brain dynamics and are related to cognitive processing | Xu, Long, Feng & Gong (2023), Nature Human Behaviour 7:1196–1215. In Human Connectome Project fMRI (100 subjects per cohort), the phase field of slow cortical fluctuations holds about 16–19 rotating spirals at a time, centred on phase singularities that drift superdiffusively and sit on boundaries between functional regions. Opposite spirals annihilate, like ones repel. Spiral locations and rotation directions decode four language-task conditions at about 48% (chance 25%, matched raw-signal decoder 30%), and spiral arrays route task activity flow bottom-up while listening and top-down while answering. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-502](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-502.md)); worth reading as the claim that slow (0.01–0.1 Hz) human cortical fMRI fluctuations self-organise into many mobile, interacting spiral waves around phase singularities, as in excitable media and turbulence, and that their locations and rotation directions are task-specific and steer large-scale activity flow. The detection is careful about filtering artefacts (phase-randomised null, filtered–unfiltered similarity); the functional claims are correlational, the spatial scale was chosen to maximise task decoding, and the "gate" and "wall" rules are read off streamlines and a phase-oscillator lattice, not tested by perturbation. |
| [LIT-640](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-640.md) | Perceptual consciousness overflows cognitive access | Block (2011), Trends in Cognitive Sciences 15(12):567–575. A defence of the overflow argument: perceptual consciousness has a higher capacity than cognitive access. Critics who call it an illusion must posit detailed unconscious iconic memory and conscious generic or fragmentary representations, for which there is no independent evidence. Fragile visual short-term memory, a cortical store of about 5–7 of 8 items over 1–4 s that attention and dlPFC TMS spare while they impair working memory, supports rich perception. Overflow means most items are not accessed, not that any is inaccessible. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-500](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-500.md)); worth reading as Block's reply to the anti-overflow critics of 2009–2011. Sparse views must posit an unconscious iconic memory detailed enough to do the Sperling and Amsterdam tasks plus conscious "generic" letters or rectangles, and Block argues there is no independent evidence for either. It adds fragile visual short-term memory (about 6–7 of 8 items at 1–2.5 s, cortical, in V4, spared by right dlPFC TMS that impairs working memory) and an imagery task as support. Read from the in-press version. |
| [LIT-641](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-641.md) | What Psychological States are Not | Block & Fodor (1972), The Philosophical Review 81(2):159–181. Behaviourism and type physicalism set type-identity conditions on psychological states that are too concrete, and the decisive arguments against them are empirical. The functional state identity theory (FSIT), on which each psychological state is a machine-table state of the organism's unique best description as a probabilistic automaton, fails too. It cannot model dispositions that are never occurrent, simultaneous states, or a productive and structured set of states, and it individuates too finely. Inverted or absent qualia are a prima facie objection to any functional definition. Psychological states look like computational states, not machine-table states, and type identity is fixed by the laws the states fall under. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-491](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-491.md)); worth reading as the first sustained case against machine-state functionalism, and as the place where the inverted- and absent-qualia objection is first set down as an objection to functional definitions of mental states. Its central result is narrower than "functionalism is false": psychological states cannot be put one-to-one with the machine-table states of a probabilistic automaton (§III, arguments 1, 2, 4, 5, 6), though they may correspond to computational states. Only the qualia argument (3) threatens functionalism in the broad sense, and the authors treat it as prima facie. |
| [LIT-642](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-642.md) | Psychologism and Behaviorism | Block (1981), The Philosophical Review 90(1):5–43. Psychologism, the doctrine that whether behaviour is intelligent depends on the information processing that produces it, is true. A machine that stores all sensible conversations of a test's length and looks up its replies has the capacity to respond sensibly to any sequence of inputs, so it satisfies the strongest behaviourist conception of intelligence, yet all its intelligence is its programmers'. The standard objections to behaviourism (Chisholm–Geach, the perfect actor, paralytics) defeat behaviourist necessary conditions but not sufficient ones; this machine defeats the sufficient condition. Psychologism is not chauvinism: it excludes one kind of processing without requiring ours. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-506](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-506.md)); worth reading as the source of the "Blockhead": a machine that stores every sensible hour-long conversation and so has the capacity to pass any Turing test of that length, yet "has the intelligence of a toaster". The argument refutes behaviourist sufficient conditions for intelligence, including a capacity version that survives the standard objections, and establishes psychologism: whether behaviour is intelligent depends partly on the processing that produces it. It does not say which processing is required, only that it needs some "richness", and the closing case against simulators of physics, neurons or psychology is admitted to be a sketch. |
| [LIT-643](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-643.md) | On a confusion about a function of consciousness | Block (1995), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 18(2):227–247, with open peer commentary. "Consciousness" is a mongrel concept. Phenomenal consciousness is experience; a state is access-conscious if its content is poised for use in reasoning and in rational control of action and speech. Arguments from blindsight and petit mal automatism to a function of phenomenal consciousness are fallacious, because access is missing in those cases too, and its machinery has the function in question. Cases of phenomenality without access (Sperling's arrays, the unnoticed drill) are offered as worth investigating, not as proven. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-493](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-493.md)); worth reading as the source of the distinction between phenomenal consciousness (P: experience, what it is like) and access consciousness (A: a content poised for use as a premise in reasoning and for rational control of action and speech). The paper's target is an argument form, not a theory: from a case where "consciousness" and some capacity are missing together (blindsight, petit mal automatism) to a function of P. In those cases A is missing too, so the obvious function of A's machinery is being credited to P. The cases of P without A that it offers (the noticed drill, Sperling's arrays, anaesthesia) are put forward as suggestive, not as evidence. |
| [LIT-644](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-644.md) | Distinct ventral stream and prefrontal cortex representational dynamics during sustained conscious visual perception | Vishne, Gerber, Knight & Deouell (2023), Cell Reports 42:112752. Ten patients with subdural electrodes watched images for 300–1,500 ms with no report on analysed trials. High-frequency activity dropped about 80% after onset in every region, but category and exemplar information in ventral temporal cortex stayed decodable and time-invariant for as long as the image stayed on. Prefrontal and parietal information was a transient burst at about 150–600 ms that did not track duration. Both IIT's and the global workspace's predictions for this paradigm held. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-499](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-499.md)); worth reading as the cleanest test in the record of what neural activity does while a seen image simply stays on. In 10 epilepsy patients with subdural electrodes, high-frequency activity falls about 80% after onset everywhere, yet category and exemplar information in ventral temporal (and less robustly occipital) cortex stays decodable, time-invariant and as long as the image, while prefrontal and parietal information is a transient burst at onset that ignores duration, with no report required. It confirms the multi-duration predictions both IIT and the global neuronal workspace made for this paradigm. Sparse frontal coverage and above-threshold stimuli only. |
| [LIT-646](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-646.md) | Consciousness, accessibility, and the mesh between psychology and neuroscience | Block (2007), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 30(5–6):481–499, with open peer commentary. To find the neural basis of experience we must decide whether it includes the machinery of cognitive access, and reports seem unable to decide that. Inference to the best explanation can. Sperling, Landman et al. and Sligte et al. show phenomenology overflowing a working memory of about four items. If the workspace is not part of the basis of phenomenology, strong losing coalitions in sensory cortex realise that overflow; the mesh between psychology and neuroscience favours that assumption. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-497](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-497.md)); worth reading as the overflow argument and the paper that framed the methodological problem the no-report paradigm was built to solve. Phenomenology overflows cognitive access: in Sperling, Landman et al. and Sligte et al. subjects see 8–32 items and can access about 4. If the neural basis of phenomenology excludes the frontal workspace, strong but losing recurrent coalitions in the back of the head explain that overflow, and a better mesh between psychology and neuroscience is reason to accept the assumption. The target article was read; the 32 commentaries and the response were not. |
| [LIT-647](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-647.md) | Neural traveling waves in cortex: Network mechanisms and potential roles in neural computation | Muller, Busch, Davis & Reynolds (2026), Neuron 114:3156–3174. A review of neural traveling waves within single cortical areas, chiefly visual cortex: how circuits generate them, and how, by embedding sensory history in the evolving activity across a sensory map, they may implement spatiotemporal computations such as predicting upcoming input. It ends with a framework for generative processing by waves over sensory maps. Unread: registered from the abstract. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 from the PubMed abstract, keywords and the Crossref record, not read. No lawful full text could be found: the article is not open access at Cell Press (Crossref gives the accepted manuscript an Elsevier open-access licence only from 2 September 2027), it is not in PubMed Central, Europe PMC lists no preprint, arXiv has none under Muller with this title, Unpaywall and OpenAlex list no repository copy, and Semantic Scholar marks it closed. The cell.com page returned a bot challenge, which was not pursued. A human reader with subscription access, or anyone after the accepted manuscript becomes open in September 2027, could read it and move this to Active. |
| [LIT-648](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-648.md) | Advertisement for a Semantics for Psychology | Block (1986), Midwest Studies in Philosophy 10:615–678. A semantics for cognitive science should explain, among other things, narrow and wide meaning, what makes expressions meaningful, the relativity of meaning to representational system, learning, and how inherited meaning (of words on a page) relates to autonomous meaning (of the language of thought). Two-factor conceptual role semantics is the only approach that promises all of them: an expression's narrow meaning is its causal role in reasoning and deliberation, short-armed at the skin, and a referential factor fixes truth conditions. Conceptual role determines the nature of the referential factor but not reference. Harman's one-factor long-arm roles collapse into the same theory; Gricean and indicator semantics are either not naturalistic or fail. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-503](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-503.md)); worth reading as the main statement of two-factor conceptual role semantics: narrow meaning is an expression's conceptual role inside the head ("total causal role, abstractly described"), and a separate referential factor relates it to the world. Block argues it is the only approach that can meet eight desiderata for a semantics serving cognitive science, among them narrow content, learning, relativity to representational system, and the relation of autonomous to inherited meaning. It is an advertisement, as titled: no identity conditions for conceptual roles are given, and Block says he is "far from a true believer". |
| [LIT-649](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-649.md) | Précis of The Border between Seeing and Thinking | Block (2024), Philosophy and Phenomenological Research 110(1):273–283, the précis for a symposium on his 2023 book. The book's main claim is that perception is constitutively iconic, nonconceptual and nonpropositional, while cognition is paradigmatically discursive, conceptual and propositional and can use perceptual material inside a "cognitive envelope". The global neuronal workspace is reread as the mechanism of that envelope, the conceptualisation of percepts. Nine kinds of evidence show working-memory representations differ from perceptual ones and are task-dependent abstractions, which increases Block's doubt that "raw" percepts are used in cognition. Iconicity is defined by tracking and mirroring conditions after Shepard. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-498](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-498.md)); worth reading as Block's own short statement, stand-in for the book ([LIT-636](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-636.md)), of the thesis of The Border Between Seeing and Thinking: perception is constitutively iconic, nonconceptual and nonpropositional, cognition paradigmatically discursive, conceptual and propositional. Despite its title it is "an update", and most of it develops one idea, the "cognitive envelope": the global workspace is better read as a theory of how percepts are conceptualised than of consciousness, and recent working-memory evidence shows percepts are recoded, not held raw, when used in reasoning. It is too short to carry the book's arguments for the main thesis, which it states but does not argue. |
| [LIT-650](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-650.md) | Conscious birds | Maldarelli & Güntürkün (2025), Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 380:20240308. A review arguing that birds show sensory awareness (bistable perception in pigeons; crow nidopallium caudolaterale neurons that follow the reported percept, not the stimulus) and graded self-awareness (magpie and house crow mark tests; pigeons and roosters that treat their mirror image as not-a-conspecific while failing the mark test). The authors say the evidence does not yet allow a strong conclusion. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-488](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-488.md)); worth reading as a short, current statement of the case for consciousness in birds and of what each of three theories (global neuronal workspace, recurrent processing, IIT) would need to find in an avian brain. Its strongest evidence is second-hand: crow nidopallium caudolaterale neurons that track the reported percept rather than the stimulus (Nieder et al. 2020). Its sharpest argument is that the bird's prefrontal analogue is nuclear, not laminar, so conscious report does not need cortical layering. The authors say the findings "do not allow for a strong conclusion". |

Against the received view that only individuals have emotions, it argues that some groups have the computational complexity and informational integration that emotion requires. Emotions are integrated, action- oriented representations built from subpersonal routines; a distributed system can integrate routines the same way. It answers the objection from consciousness (some individual emotions are non-conscious, so collective ones need not be felt) and from homology (emotion kinds are functional, "like vodka", not "like bourbon"). An emotion is an integrated representation with indicative content and imperative force, built from subpersonal routines; a group whose routines are integrated the same way can be in one, without feeling it. The test case fails on the author's own terms (the USS Palau crew detects danger without fear) and the replacement (a 2008 presidential campaign) is offered as intuitively plausible pending anthropology, so the paper establishes a possibility and a research programme, not an instance. |

In mouse cortex during one overtrained decision task, a covariance-matched Gaussian null is beaten within single areas only in a few primary sensory ones, while the task conditions each area tells apart are linearly separable in nearly every balanced split. Neuron types appear when areas are pooled, and track anatomy. Second reading under [ADR-013](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-013.md); the anthology holds it as [ANTH-LIT-696](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/blob/main/record/literature.d/LIT-696.md), read for concept geometry in ML. |
| [LIT-736](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-736.md) | Shaping the Institutional Mind | Tollefsen (2025), Philosophies 10(5):112. Advocates and critics of group minds share the "standard view" that ascribing attitudes tracks pre-existing causes. On McGeer's regulative view, ascription shapes its target. Ascribing knowledge to institutions, as in the collective knowledge doctrine, and issuing institutional narratives shape institutions to be more agent-like. The view stays agnostic about whether institutions really have minds. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-570](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-570.md)): in full, from the publisher's open-access PDF (CC BY 4.0). Worth reading for a different answer to why we ascribe beliefs and knowledge to institutions: not because the ascriptions describe pre-existing states, but because, on the regulative view of folk psychology, they shape institutions to be more agent-like. Its main case is the collective knowledge doctrine in corporate criminal law, after which banks built systems to detect reporting violations. Limits: the regulative view is assumed, not argued; the causal story about banks is asserted without evidence; and the paper is agnostic about whether institutions have minds. It does not stand in for her book Groups as Agents ([LIT-483](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-483.md)), which stays unread. |

Not read: no lawful full text was found. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-09 from catalogue records, not read: no lawful full text was found. | [LIT-769](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-769.md) | Language Evolution by Iterated Learning With Bayesian Agents | Griffiths & Kalish (2007), Cognitive Science 31(3):441–480. When Bayesian learners sample a language from their posterior, iterated learning is a Gibbs sampler and converges to the learners' prior; when they take the posterior mode, it behaves like a variant of EM and depends also on how much data passes between generations; in a two-language case the MAP outcome is the same for a wide range of prior strengths. Read in [NOTE-599](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-599.md). | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-599](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-599.md)); worth reading as the analytic result behind iterated learning: a chain of learners who share a prior and each sample a hypothesis from their posterior is a Gibbs sampler, so the probability that a learner holds a language converges to its prior probability whatever the amount of data passed on, and the data produced converge to the prior predictive. Learners who take the MAP hypothesis run stochastic EM instead: the outcome centres on the prior's mode but depends on data amount and noise, and in the two-language case is the same for every prior strength α between 0.5 and 1 − ε, so weak biases can be amplified. Equal-fitness populations share the equilibrium. Source of [THEORY-155](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-155.md). |

Artificial languages passed down chains of human learners become easier to learn and more structured, without any learner intending it: cultural transmission produces design without a designer. Without a pressure against ambiguity the languages collapse into a few words for classes of meanings; with homonyms filtered from training they become compositional. Skimmed in [NOTE-596](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-596.md). | Active — skimmed 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-596](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-596.md)): every section of the main text was covered, but through a fetch tool's section-by-section account of the PubMed Central page, not a verbatim copy, and the SI was not reached; worth reading as the laboratory demonstration of iterated learning: four chains of ten adults, each learning a 27-item artificial language from 14 items and passing on its test output, made the languages steadily easier to learn and more structured while believing they were copying. | [LIT-777](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-777.md) | Context–content systems of random variables: The Contextuality-by-Default theory | Dzhafarov & Kujala (2016), J. Math. Psychol. 74:11–33. Contextuality-by-Default for finite systems of categorical random variables, indexed by content and context. A system is noncontextual when some coupling of its context bunches makes every connection a maximal coupling; the test is a linear program, the binary cyclic criterion is stated (proved elsewhere), and the minimal total variation of a signed maximally connected quasi-coupling, minus 1, measures the degree of contextuality. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-600](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-600.md)); worth reading as the reference statement of Contextuality-by-Default: each measurement gets a separate random variable in each context, and a system is noncontextual when some coupling of its contexts makes every content's copies coincide as often as their own distributions allow (maximal couplings). This separates context-dependent marginals ("direct influences") from contextuality, turns the test into linear-programming feasibility (Theorem 4.1), and, since a signed such coupling always exists (Theorem 6.1), measures contextuality as the least total variation above 1. The definition was already being replaced by "multimaximal" couplings when it appeared (footnote 10). |
| [LIT-790](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-790.md) | Contextuality in Canonical Systems of Random Variables | Dzhafarov, Cervantes & Kujala (2017), Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 375:20160389. Proposes that contextuality be judged only on a system's canonical representation: every variable, and every joining or coarsening of interest, replaced by its binary splits, with connections coupled multimaximally (pairwise maximally). For two content-sharing k-valued variables with all splits kept, the canonical system is noncontextual if and only if one variable nominally dominates the other (Pr below the other's for at most one value; Theorem 4.6). For continuous densities with all splits, any difference in distribution is contextual. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-640](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-640.md)); worth reading as the step that makes Contextuality-by-Default representation-dependent. Every variable is replaced by binary splits (dichotomizations) and connections are coupled multimaximally, so a verdict belongs to a chosen set of splits, not to the measurements alone. Its one worked result is striking: if every split of two content-sharing k-valued variables is kept, that pair alone is noncontextual exactly when one variable "nominally dominates" the other, i.e. its probabilities fall below the other's for at most one value (Theorem 4.6). For continuous variables the analogue makes any difference in distribution count as contextuality. The authors present this as opening behavioural contextuality, not as a reductio. Proofs are in the supplement and contain small slips that do not affect the results. |
| [LIT-795](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-795.md) | Context effects produced by question orders reveal quantum nature of human judgments | Wang, Solloway, Shiffrin & Busemeyer (2014), PNAS 111(26):9431–9436. Tests the QQ equality of [LIT-834](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-834.md), that the probability of giving the same answer to two questions does not depend on their order, on 70 national surveys and two laboratory experiments. Across all 66 Pew surveys from 2001–2011 that varied the order of two questions, order effects are significant (p = 0.0004) and the q values are not (p = 0.4625); paired context effects across 72 studies correlate at r = −0.82 along the predicted line of slope −1. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-604](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-604.md)); worth reading as the large-scale test of the QQ equality: across 66 Pew surveys chosen without regard to their results, question order changes the answers significantly (p = 0.0004 for the distribution of order-effect χ² values), while the probability of answering the two questions alike stays the same (p = 0.4625 for the q values). Read with the caveats that the supporting information, which holds the proof, the per-study table and the χ² tests, was not reachable and was not read, and that the paper's title claims more than its evidence: the equality is a symmetry constraint that the authors concede a classical model could be built to satisfy, and [LIT-264](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-264.md) shows that data satisfying it are noncontextual. |

The review that names and states the rational speech act framework: a listener interprets an utterance by Bayesian inversion of an approximately rational speaker who values informativeness to a literal listener, replacing Grice's maxims with one utility-theoretic cooperative principle; joint inference over the speaker's topic, knowledge or lexicon (uRSA) extends it to non-literal language, vagueness and embedded implicature. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-606](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-606.md)), from the authors' manuscript; worth reading as the standard statement of the rational speech act (RSA) framework: a pragmatic listener P_L(w\|u) ∝ P_S(u\|w)P(w) inverting a softmax speaker whose utility is log P_Lit(w\|u), with a literal listener conditioning the prior on the utterance's truth. Its uncertain-RSA extension, a joint posterior over the world and the speaker's type, topic or lexicon, is what carries hyperbole, irony, metaphor, vague adjectives and embedded implicature.
